title: Diseases and medicines: what causes an illness, what a medicine does, and how we know it works

summary.text: Twelve limp coriander stems go into two glasses. One glass holds plain water. The other holds sugar water, which some people say revives greens. Two hours later, the stems in both glasses stand up about equally well. Seen alone, the sugar glass would have looked like a cure. A cold is similar: it ends in about a week with a remedy, and in about a week without one. Every disease has a cause, such as a germ, a missing nutrient or a failing body part. A medicine can remove the cause, replace what is missing, ease the symptoms or prevent the disease. Your child adds doses of tea to a glass of water that stands for a body, and tracks the level. They run a fair trial on wilted stems. They learn how doctors test a medicine. They also learn why a medicine is given only by a grown-up, in the way a doctor says.
summary.art: Two clear glasses on a kitchen counter, each holding six coriander stems standing upright, with a spoon of sugar beside one glass and a notebook tally between them.

intro.hook: A cold goes away about a week after you take a remedy. A cold also goes away about a week after you take nothing. So how can anyone find out whether a remedy works?
intro.text: People have used remedies for thousands of years, and many of them did nothing. For about two thousand years, doctors let blood out of ill people, and it harmed far more than it helped. Nobody could tell, because many ill people get better whatever is done to them. In this unit you find out how people learned to tell a real medicine from a useless one. First you learn that every disease has a cause, and that a treatment must fit the cause. You use a glass of water and spoons of tea as a model of a body. You see how a medicine builds up there and leaves. You run a fair trial on wilted coriander stems, with a remedy group and a comparison group. You test whether a label changes how sweet a drink tastes. No real medicine is used anywhere in this unit. Medicines are only for a grown-up to give, in the way a doctor says. By the end you can say what a medicine can do and what only the body can do. You can also say what counts as evidence that a medicine works.
intro.art: A child looking at two glasses of coriander stems on a table, one glass marked A and one marked B on slips of paper tucked under them.

outcomes: By the end I can name five kinds of cause of disease, and say why treatment must fit the cause.
By the end I can match common diseases and deficiency diseases to their cause and their protection.
By the end I can say the four jobs a medicine can do, and what only the body can do.
By the end I can explain how a medicine travels through the body and leaves it. I can say why a dose has an amount and a time.
By the end I can explain why getting better after a remedy does not show that the remedy worked.
By the end I can say what a fair trial of a medicine needs: two like groups, chance, a dummy, blind measuring and many people.
By the end I can give the rules for medicines at home, starting with this one: only a grown-up gives a medicine, as a doctor says.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about, such as how much a dummy tablet can do.

terms.meaning: A condition in which part of the body, or the mind, does not work as it should, for some time.
terms.example: Malaria, anaemia, diabetes and asthma are all diseases, and each has a different cause.
terms.art: Four small pictures in a row: a person shivering under a blanket, a pale tired child, a finger-prick blood test and an inhaler.

terms.meaning: The thing that makes a disease begin. Take the cause away early enough, and the disease does not happen.
terms.example: The cause of malaria is a tiny parasite passed on by a mosquito. The cause of goitre is too little iodine.
terms.art: A mosquito on an arm on the left and a pinch of salt on the right, each with an arrow pointing to a tired person in the middle.

terms.meaning: A change that an ill person feels or shows, such as fever, pain, a cough or tiredness.
terms.example: A fever is a symptom. Malaria, flu and typhoid can each cause it, so a fever alone does not name the disease.
terms.art: A child in bed with a thermometer, and three faint question marks above labelled with a mosquito, a cough and a glass of water.

terms.meaning: Finding out which disease a person has, and what caused it. A doctor asks questions, examines the body and may order tests.
terms.example: A doctor sends a drop of blood to be tested for malaria parasites before choosing a medicine.
terms.art: A doctor looking into a microscope, with a glass slide holding one drop of blood beside her.

terms.meaning: A disease caused by too little of one nutrient for a long time.
terms.example: Too little iron causes anaemia. Too little vitamin C causes scurvy.
terms.art: A plate of plain white rice on one side and a bunch of greens with a lemon on the other, with an arrow from the greens to a tired girl.

terms.meaning: A disease that lasts for years, and that medicines can control but usually cannot end. Doctors also say 'chronic disease'.
terms.example: Diabetes and asthma are long-term diseases. A person takes medicine for them for many years and lives a full life.
terms.art: A grandmother checking her blood sugar with a small meter at a table, with a calendar on the wall behind her.

terms.meaning: A substance used to treat, ease or prevent a disease. A medicine is also called a drug.
terms.example: An antibiotic, a vaccine, an iron tablet and an asthma inhaler are all medicines, and each does a different job.
terms.art: A closed medicine box on a high shelf, with a tablet strip, a syrup bottle and an inhaler drawn in outline on its side.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them multiplying. An antibiotic does nothing to viruses.
terms.example: A doctor may give an antibiotic for typhoid, which bacteria cause. A virus causes a cold, so an antibiotic cannot help a cold.
terms.art: A strip of tablets with a red line down its back, beside a drawing of rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: The amount of a medicine to be given at one time. The doctor or the label also says how often.
terms.example: A label may say 5 millilitres, three times a day. The 5 millilitres is the dose.
terms.art: A small measuring cup with lines on its side, filled to the line marked 5 ml.

terms.meaning: All the doses of a medicine that a doctor orders for one illness, from the first to the last.
terms.example: A course may be one tablet twice a day for five days. That is ten tablets in all.
terms.art: A tablet strip with ten tablets beside a small calendar with five days ringed.

terms.meaning: The time a body takes to remove half of a medicine that is in the blood.
terms.example: A medicine has a half-life of 4 hours. Half of a dose is left after 4 hours, and a quarter after 8 hours.
terms.art: Three glasses in a row holding brown liquid that is dark, then paler, then very pale, with a clock between each pair.

terms.meaning: An effect of a medicine that nobody wanted, such as sleepiness, a rash or a stomach ache.
terms.example: Some cold medicines make people sleepy. Sleepiness is a side effect of those medicines.
terms.art: A person yawning at a desk, with a small tablet strip beside a glass of water.

terms.meaning: A doctor's written order for a medicine. It names the medicine, the dose, the times and the number of days.
terms.example: The chemist reads the prescription before selling an antibiotic.
terms.art: A slip of paper headed with the letters Rx, with three lines of writing, held by a chemist behind a counter.

terms.meaning: The name of the substance in a medicine that does the work. Many companies sell the same substance under their own brand names.
terms.example: Paracetamol is a generic name. It is sold in India under dozens of brand names.
terms.art: Two tablet strips with different bright brand names on the front and the same small-print name on the back.

terms.meaning: An illness that the body ends by its own defences and repair, usually within days.
terms.example: A common cold is self-limiting. Most colds are over in seven to ten days, with or without a remedy.
terms.art: A row of seven small calendar squares with a child's face in each, sniffling in the first and smiling in the last.

terms.meaning: A test of a medicine on people who agree to take part. Its results are counted and compared.
terms.example: In a trial in 1948, patients with tuberculosis were put into two groups by chance. One group was given a new medicine.
terms.art: Two groups of patients in hospital beds, with a nurse writing numbers on a chart between them.

terms.meaning: The group in a trial that does not get the new treatment. The treated group is compared with this group.
terms.example: In the Wilted Stems Trial, the stems in plain water are the control group.
terms.art: Two glasses of stems side by side, one labelled 'remedy' and one labelled 'control'.

terms.meaning: Decided by chance alone, such as a coin toss, so that nobody's choice can tilt the result.
terms.example: A coin toss sends each stem to glass A or glass B. So the fresher stems cannot all end up in one glass.
terms.art: A hand tossing a coin above a row of coriander stems laid on a plate.

terms.meaning: A dummy treatment that looks like the real one and holds no medicine. Trials use it for the control group.
terms.example: In a trial, half the people may get the real tablet and half a tablet made of plain starch. The starch tablet is the placebo.
terms.art: Two tablets that look exactly the same, one with a tiny label 'medicine' and the other with a tiny label 'starch only'.

terms.meaning: A test in which the people being tested do not know which treatment they got. Often the people who measure do not know either.
terms.example: In the Label Test, the second round is blind, because the cups carry no labels.
terms.art: Two plain steel tumblers with small letters hidden on their bases, and a taster with a puzzled, thoughtful face.

terms.meaning: Facts, counts or measurements that show whether a claim is true.
terms.example: 'My cousin took it and got well' is weak evidence. 'Of 55 people who took it, 51 lived' is stronger evidence.
terms.art: A notebook page with two columns of tally marks and a total written under each.

terms.meaning: Stopping a disease before it starts, by blocking its cause.
terms.example: Iodised salt prevents goitre. A mosquito net prevents malaria. A vaccine prevents measles.
terms.art: A packet of iodised salt, a folded mosquito net and a vaccine card laid side by side.

explanations.concept: Every disease has a cause, and treatment starts by finding it
explanations.context: This card says why a doctor asks so many questions before choosing a medicine.
explanations.definition: A symptom is what an illness shows. A cause is what makes the illness begin. A treatment works only if it fits the cause.
explanations.description: Fever, tiredness, cough and stomach ache are symptoms. One symptom can come from many causes. A fever may come from malaria, typhoid, dengue, flu or an infected tooth. Each of these needs a different treatment, and some need no medicine at all. So a doctor first finds the cause. This is called diagnosis. The doctor asks when the illness began, what the person ate and where they travelled. The doctor looks, listens and feels, and may order a test of blood, urine or spit. A medicine chosen without a diagnosis is a guess. A wrong guess wastes days, and the real cause goes on working. A medicine that only hides a symptom can also hide the clue the doctor needs.
examples: A fever with shivering every second day points to malaria, and a blood test confirms it.
Tiredness may come from anaemia, poor sleep, diabetes or tuberculosis. Each has a different treatment.
A cough that lasts more than two weeks needs a test for tuberculosis. Cough syrup will not show the cause.
explanations.art: A doctor listening to a child's chest with a stethoscope while the mother points to a calendar on the wall.

explanations.context: This card sorts the causes of disease into five kinds. Each kind needs a different sort of answer.
explanations.definition: A disease may be caused by a germ, a missing nutrient or a body part that stops working well. Harm from outside and an inherited fault are causes too.
explanations.description: First, germs. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites enter the body and multiply. Cholera, malaria and tuberculosis begin this way. Second, a missing nutrient. A body short of iron, iodine or a vitamin for months falls ill. These are deficiency diseases. Third, a body part that stops working well. In type 1 diabetes, the cells of the pancreas that make insulin are destroyed. In a cataract, the lens of the eye turns cloudy with age. Fourth, harm from outside and from the way we live. Tobacco smoke, dirty air, alcohol, too little movement and too much sugar and salt damage the body slowly. Fifth, an inherited fault. A child gets it from the parents in their genes, as in sickle cell disease. Many diseases have two causes working together. Tuberculosis needs the germ, and the disease strikes hardest where people are short of food.
examples: Diseases caused by germs include typhoid, dengue, measles and ringworm.
Diseases caused by a missing nutrient include anaemia, goitre, rickets and scurvy.
Diseases caused by a body part that stops working well include type 1 diabetes and cataract.
Diseases caused by harm from outside include lung disease from tobacco smoke and many heart attacks.
Diseases that are inherited include sickle cell disease and thalassaemia.
explanations.art: Five small panels in a row: a germ under a lens, an empty plate with one grain, a pancreas with a few dim cells, a smoking chimney, and a family tree with two marked squares.

explanations.concept: Common infectious diseases: the germ, the road and the protection
explanations.context: This card lists the infectious diseases that Class 5 books in India name. For each disease the card gives the germ, the germ's road and the protection.
explanations.definition: An infectious disease is caused by a germ. The germ reaches a person by a certain road, and blocking that road prevents the disease.
explanations.description: Cholera, typhoid and most diarrhoea come from germs in dirty water and food. Safe water, cooked food, a toilet and soap stop them. A child with loose motions needs oral rehydration solution, called ORS, and a doctor if they cannot drink. Malaria is caused by a parasite, and female Anopheles mosquitoes carry the parasite. Dengue is caused by a virus, carried by Aedes mosquitoes, who bite in the day. Filariasis is caused by thin worms, also carried by mosquitoes, and it can make a leg swell greatly. Nets, covered water and no standing puddles stop all three. Tuberculosis, flu, colds, measles and pneumonia travel in the air from coughs and sneezes. Fresh air, covered coughs and vaccines stop many of them. HIV is a virus passed on by infected blood, and from a mother to her baby. HIV is not passed on by touching, sharing food or mosquitoes. Medicines now keep people with HIV well for a full life.
examples: Cholera and typhoid are caused by bacteria, and they spread through water and food. Typhoid has a vaccine and is treated with an antibiotic.
Malaria is caused by a parasite, and mosquitoes carry the parasite from person to person. A blood test confirms malaria, and antimalarial medicines treat it.
Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium and spreads through the air. Several medicines taken together for at least six months cure the disease. They are free at government centres.
Measles and polio are caused by viruses. Both are prevented by vaccines given to babies.
explanations.art: A chart with three columns headed water and food, mosquito and air, with a tap, a mosquito and a cough drawn at the top and small disease names below.

explanations.concept: Deficiency diseases: the cure is the missing nutrient
explanations.context: This card is about diseases caused by a missing nutrient. No medicine that kills germs can cure them.
explanations.definition: A deficiency disease is caused by too little of one nutrient for a long time. It is cured and prevented by supplying that nutrient.
explanations.description: Too little iron causes anaemia. The blood carries less oxygen, and the person is pale, tired and breathless. Too little vitamin A causes night blindness. Too little vitamin D or calcium causes rickets, in which a child's leg bones bend. Too little iodine causes goitre, a swelling at the front of the neck. Too little vitamin B1 causes beriberi, which weakens the legs and the heart. Too little vitamin C causes scurvy, with bleeding gums. Small children who get far too little protein and energy develop kwashiorkor or marasmus. Kwashiorkor shows as swollen feet, and marasmus as extreme thinness. For centuries people looked for a germ or bad air behind these diseases, and found none. The cause was something absent. The treatment is the nutrient itself, from food, from fortified food such as iodised salt, or from tablets. Iron and vitamin tablets are medicines too. Too many can poison a child, so a doctor decides the dose.
examples: Anaemia is prevented by iron from ragi, bajra, chana and greens, eaten with lemon. A doctor may add iron tablets.
Night blindness is prevented by vitamin A from drumstick leaves, carrot, papaya and mango.
Goitre is prevented by iodine from iodised salt.
Beriberi is prevented by vitamin B1 from unpolished rice, whole grains and dals.
explanations.art: A table with two columns: on the left a pale face, a bent leg bone and a swollen neck, and on the right greens with lemon, sunshine with milk, and a packet of iodised salt.

explanations.concept: Long-term diseases: medicines that control and do not cure
explanations.context: This card is about diseases that last for years, such as diabetes and asthma. Their medicines work in a different way from an antibiotic.
explanations.definition: A long-term disease stays for years. Its medicine does the work of a failing part, or holds the symptoms down. This lasts only while the medicine is taken.
explanations.description: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops making insulin. Insulin is the hormone that lets sugar pass from the blood into the cells. Before 1922, a child with this disease lived only a year or two. In January 1922 doctors in Toronto, Canada, injected insulin into Leonard Thompson, a boy of 14, and he lived. Insulin does not repair the pancreas. It replaces what the pancreas no longer makes, every day. In type 2 diabetes the body makes insulin but responds to it poorly. Food, exercise and tablets control it. About ten crore people in India have diabetes. In asthma, the airways of the lungs swell and tighten. One inhaler opens the airways within minutes. Another, used daily, keeps the swelling down. High blood pressure is controlled by daily tablets, which lowers the chance of a heart attack or a stroke. Cancer is treated by surgery, by medicines and by radiation. Not smoking, moving every day and eating well lower the chance of many long-term diseases.
examples: Insulin injections replace the insulin that the pancreas no longer makes.
A reliever inhaler opens tight airways in an asthma attack. A preventer inhaler is used every day.
A person with high blood pressure may take one tablet daily for decades and stay well.
explanations.art: A girl of about twelve holding an inhaler with a spacer, and beside her an older man testing a drop of blood on a small meter.

explanations.concept: What a medicine does, and what only the body can do
explanations.context: This card says what the four jobs of a medicine are. It also says which part of getting well is always done by the body.
explanations.definition: A medicine removes a cause, replaces something missing, eases a symptom or prevents a disease. The body does the repair.
explanations.description: An antibiotic kills bacteria or stops them multiplying. The body's own defenders then clear what is left, and the body mends the damaged tissue. An iron tablet supplies iron, and the bone marrow builds the new blood cells. ORS replaces lost water and salts, while the gut clears the germ and regrows the gut lining. Paracetamol lowers a fever and dulls pain, so a child can rest and drink. It does nothing to the cause. A vaccine shows the defenders a harmless part of a germ, and the defenders build the protection. A doctor's stitches hold the edges of a deep cut together. The skin cells then join the edges, and no medicine does that for them. A plaster cast holds a broken bone still, and the bone knits itself. So in every treatment, the medicine does one exact job. The body does the mending.
examples: Stitches hold a cut closed. New skin cells join the edges in about a week.
An antibiotic lowers the number of bacteria. White blood cells clear the rest.
A cast holds a child's broken arm still for four to six weeks while bone cells bridge the break.
explanations.art: An arm in a plaster cast beside a cut-away drawing of the bone inside, with new bone bridging a crack.

explanations.concept: How a medicine reaches the place where it works
explanations.context: This card follows a swallowed tablet through the body. It also says why some medicines are breathed in, dropped in or rubbed on.
explanations.definition: A swallowed medicine dissolves in the gut, passes into the blood and is carried to every part of the body.
explanations.description: A tablet breaks up in the stomach and dissolves. In the small intestine the dissolved medicine passes through the gut wall into the blood. The blood goes first to the liver, and then the heart pumps it everywhere. This takes about half an hour to an hour. The medicine reaches the sore throat, and also the toes, the skin and the brain. A medicine acts only where its molecules fit. Each kind of medicine molecule fits one kind of molecule in the body or in a germ. A key fits a lock in a similar way. Some medicines are put straight where they are needed. An inhaler sends a mist into the lungs, so its dose can be about thirty times smaller than a tablet's. Eye drops go on the eye and ointment on the skin. An injection puts medicine into a muscle or a vein, for medicines that the stomach would destroy. Insulin is one of these.
examples: A syrup acts a little sooner than a tablet, because it is already dissolved.
A puff from an asthma inhaler holds a tiny dose, and nearly all of it goes to the lungs.
Insulin is a protein. The stomach would digest it like food, so it is injected.
explanations.art: An outline of a child's body with a dotted path from mouth to stomach to intestine to liver to heart and out to the whole body.

explanations.concept: How a medicine leaves the body, and why doses are spaced
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Half-Glass Test, where half the tea was poured away at every turn.
explanations.definition: The liver changes a medicine and the kidneys pass it out in urine. The time taken to remove half of it is called its half-life.
explanations.description: The body starts to remove a medicine as soon as it arrives. The liver changes the molecules, and the kidneys filter them into the urine. For most medicines, the body removes about half of whatever is there in a fixed time. This time is the half-life. It is about an hour for some medicines and several days for others. After one half-life, half is left. After two, a quarter is left. So one dose fades below the level that works, and another dose is needed. In the Half-Glass Test, each pour removed half of the tea, and each dose added 2 teaspoons. The tea in the glass rose to nearly 4 teaspoons and stayed there. A fuller glass loses more at each pour, so the level stops rising. Makers of a medicine use this sum to set the dose and the gap between doses. The gap keeps the level between too little and too much.
examples: In the Half-Glass Test, the glass held 2 teaspoons of tea after the first dose, then 3, then 3 and a half. It never went above 4 teaspoons.
A medicine with a short half-life may be given three or four times a day.
A medicine with a long half-life may be given once a day, or once a week.
explanations.art: A clear glass of pale brown water with a FULL line and a HALF line, and a line graph beside it that climbs in saw-teeth and levels off.

explanations.concept: The dose: enough to work, and too little to harm
explanations.context: This card is about the amount of a medicine. The same medicine can fail, help or harm, depending on the amount in the body.
explanations.definition: A dose is the amount given at one time. The right dose keeps the medicine in the blood above the level that works and below the level that harms.
explanations.description: With too little medicine in the blood, nothing happens. With too much, the medicine harms the body. Too much paracetamol damages the liver, and too many iron tablets can kill a small child. For some medicines the safe range is wide, and for others it is narrow. The right dose depends on the body. A child weighs less than a grown-up, so the same tablet makes a stronger mixture in a child's blood. A child's liver and kidneys also clear some medicines at a different speed. So a child's dose is worked out from the child's weight, and it is never a guess. In the Half-Glass Test, a double dose at every turn took the tea up towards 8 teaspoons. That is twice the level of the single doses. Taking doses closer together does the same. This is why nobody takes two doses at once to make up for a missed one. The grown-up reads the label, or asks the doctor or the chemist.
examples: A child of 15 kilograms and a grown-up of 60 kilograms may take the same medicine. Their doses differ.
In the Half-Glass Test, when every dose was doubled, the level of tea in the glass doubled too.
Iron tablets look like sweets to a toddler, so they are kept locked away.
explanations.art: Three glasses of tea water from pale to very dark, labelled 'too little', 'works' and 'too much'.

explanations.concept: Side effects: a medicine goes everywhere
explanations.context: This card explains why a medicine for one part of the body can cause an effect in another part.
explanations.definition: A side effect is an effect of a medicine that nobody wanted. It happens because the blood carries the medicine to every part of the body.
explanations.description: The blood cannot deliver a tablet to the throat alone. The medicine reaches every organ, and its molecules may fit a lock in more than one place. Some medicines for a runny nose also act on the brain and cause sleepiness. An antibiotic kills the harmful bacteria, and also many helpful bacteria in the gut. So the antibiotic may cause loose motions. A few people are allergic to a medicine. Their defenders attack it, and the result can be a rash or trouble breathing. Every medicine that has an effect can have a side effect. So a doctor weighs the good against the harm for each patient. A medicine that is right for one person may be wrong for a pregnant woman or a baby. Anyone who gets a rash, swelling or trouble breathing after a medicine must tell a grown-up at once.
examples: A medicine for a blocked nose may make a person sleepy.
An antibiotic may cause loose motions, because helpful gut bacteria die too.
A person allergic to penicillin carries a card that says so.
explanations.art: An outline of a body with a tablet's path shown as dots reaching the nose, the brain, the gut and the skin at once.

explanations.concept: Getting better anyway: why a remedy seems to work
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Wilted Stems Trial. There, stems in plain water recovered as well as stems in sugar water.
explanations.definition: Many illnesses end by the body's own defences and repair. A remedy taken during such an illness gets the credit, whether it did anything or not.
explanations.description: A cold lasts about seven to ten days. A sore throat, a small cut, a bruise and most stomach upsets also end without treatment. Such an illness is called self-limiting. Now think about when people take a remedy. They take it on the day they feel worst. After the worst day, the illness is already on the way down. So the next day feels better, and the remedy seems to have worked. People also remember the times a remedy was followed by recovery, and forget the other times. In the Wilted Stems Trial, sugar water alone would have looked like a cure. The glass of plain water showed that the stems recovered just as well without sugar. For about two thousand years, doctors bled ill people, and both doctors and patients were sure that it helped. Most of the patients who recovered would have recovered anyway.
examples: A child drinks pepper rasam on the worst day of a cold and feels better two days later. The cold was already ending.
A wart often disappears by itself within two years, so many wart remedies seem to work.
In the Wilted Stems Trial, plain water and sugar water revived about the same number of stems.
explanations.art: A line graph of how bad a cold feels over ten days, rising to a peak on day three and falling, with a small spoon drawn at the peak.

explanations.concept: The fair trial: how doctors find out whether a medicine works
explanations.context: This card says how a new medicine is tested on people. The Wilted Stems Trial used the same steps.
explanations.definition: A fair trial compares people who get a treatment with similar people who do not. Chance decides who is in which group.
explanations.description: A trial needs five things. First, two groups, a treated group and a control group, so that getting better anyway happens in both. Second, chance decides who joins which group. If the doctor chose, the doctor might give the new medicine to the stronger patients without meaning to. Third, the control group gets a placebo. This is a dummy that looks and tastes like the medicine, so nobody can tell the groups apart. Fourth, the test is blind. The patients do not know which they got, and the people who measure do not know either. Fifth, many people take part, because a few can mislead by luck. At the end the two groups are counted and compared. Every person must agree to take part, and a trial is stopped early if one group is clearly being harmed. In India, new medicines and vaccines must pass such trials before they are sold.
examples: In 1948, 107 patients with tuberculosis were put into two groups by random numbers. Streptomycin clearly saved lives.
From 1956, a trial in Madras, now Chennai, compared treatment at home and in hospital. Tuberculosis medicines worked as well at home.
A trial of India's Rotavac vaccine gave it or a placebo to 6,799 babies in Delhi, Pune and Vellore.
explanations.art: Two rows of people each holding an identical white tablet, with a coin above them and a doctor holding a sealed envelope.

explanations.concept: The placebo effect: how much can a dummy do?
explanations.context: This card is about something scientists still argue over. People who are given a dummy treatment often say that they feel better.
explanations.definition: A placebo is a dummy treatment with no medicine in it. People given one often say they feel better. Scientists disagree about how much a placebo really changes.
explanations.description: In trials, many people in the placebo group report less pain or feel less ill. Part of this is getting better anyway. Part of it may be real: expecting relief can change how the brain handles pain. In the Label Test, a label alone may have changed how sweet a drink tasted to your tasters. In 2011, doctors tested this on people with asthma. A dummy inhaler made them feel as much better as the real inhaler did. But when their breathing was measured, only the real inhaler had opened their airways. So a placebo can change what a person feels and reports. Whether a placebo can change a disease is much less sure. This is why a trial measures the body as well as asking the patient, and why it is blind.
examples: In the 2011 asthma trial, people felt better after a dummy inhaler, but their measured breathing did not improve.
A plaster on a small scrape often stops a child's crying before any healing has happened.
In the Label Test, write here whether the label changed your tasters' scores.

perspectives.who: Henry Beecher, an American doctor, in 1955
perspectives.explanation: He added up fifteen trials and wrote that about one patient in three got real relief from a placebo. He called the placebo powerful.

perspectives.who: Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche, Danish doctors, in 2001
perspectives.explanation: They studied 114 trials that also had a group given nothing at all. People given nothing improved nearly as much. They found only a small effect, mostly on pain and on what patients said about how they felt.

perspectives.who: Ted Kaptchuk, an American researcher, in 2010
perspectives.explanation: He gave people with a painful gut disease dummy pills and told them truthfully that the pills were dummies. They still reported more relief than people given nothing. He thinks the care and the routine of treatment matter in themselves.

explanations.art: Two identical inhalers on a table and a breathing meter between them, with one dial high and one dial low.

explanations.context: This card is about remedies from Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and family kitchens. People disagree about how they should be judged.
explanations.definition: An old remedy is a treatment handed down in a medical tradition or a family. Some work, some do nothing and a few do harm. People disagree about how to judge them.
explanations.description: Some of the best modern medicines began as old remedies. In India, the root of the sarpagandha plant was given for centuries to calm people. In 1931 two Indian doctors, Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose, reported that it lowered blood pressure. In 1949 Dr Rustom Jal Vakil of Bombay tested the root on patients. A medicine made from the root was soon used across the world. In 1972 Tu Youyou in China found the malaria medicine artemisinin. She had tested a plant named in a book 1,600 years old. In about 1916 Alice Ball, a young chemist in Hawaii, is credited with a way to change chaulmoogra oil so that the body could absorb it from an injection. The oil was an old Indian remedy for leprosy, and her method was used for decades. She died young, and for some years her name was left off the work. Other old remedies failed when tested, and bloodletting was one of them. A few do harm. In 2004 a study found lead, mercury or arsenic in one in five Ayurvedic products bought in shops in Boston. So age does not show that a remedy works, and 'natural' does not show that a remedy is safe.
examples: Sarpagandha root gave the world a medicine for high blood pressure, after it was tested.
Honey eases a child's night cough a little, as a trial in 2007 showed. Honey is never given to a baby under one year.
Datura is a wild plant, and their seeds are a strong poison.

perspectives.explanation: Every remedy, old or new, must pass the same fair trial. Until it does, nobody knows whether it works or what harm it does. A remedy that passes is simply called a medicine.

perspectives.who: Many physicians of Ayurveda and Siddha
perspectives.explanation: These systems treat the whole person with food, daily routine and mixtures of many plants, chosen for each patient. A trial that gives one extract to everyone does not test what they really do. Centuries of careful practice are evidence too.

perspectives.who: Scientists who search old texts, as Tu Youyou did
perspectives.explanation: Old remedies are a list of good guesses made by careful observers. Most will fail a trial, and a few will become important medicines. So the old books should be read and tested, and neither worshipped nor thrown away.

explanations.art: A sarpagandha plant with red and black berries beside an old palm-leaf manuscript and a modern blood pressure cuff.

explanations.context: This card is about a new field of study. Scientists have watched other animals treat their own illnesses with plants.
explanations.definition: Some animals eat or apply particular plants when they are ill. Scientists call this self-medication. They are still working out how the animals know what to take.
explanations.description: People are not the only animals who use medicines. In 1987, at Mahale in Tanzania, a chimpanzee named Chausiku was ill, with a bad stomach and little strength. She chewed the bitter pith of a shrub that chimpanzees normally avoid, and she swallowed only the juice. A day later she was eating and travelling again. Mohamedi Seifu Kalunde, a Tanzanian park worker, was watching with the scientist Michael Huffman. He knew the shrub as a strong medicine. In 2022, in Sumatra, an orangutan named Rakus had a deep wound on his face. He chewed the leaves of a climbing plant. He put the juice and then the mash on the wound. The wound closed in about a week. People in Southeast Asia use the same plant as a traditional medicine. Woolly bear caterpillars with parasites inside them eat more of certain bitter leaves, and more of them survive. Scientists agree on what these animals did. They still argue about how the animals know what to take.
examples: Chausiku the chimpanzee chewed a bitter pith when she had a stomach illness.
Rakus the orangutan put chewed leaves on his own wound.
Many dogs and cats eat grass. Nobody is yet sure whether grass is their medicine.

perspectives.who: Michael Huffman and other scientists who study animal self-medication
perspectives.explanation: Apes choose a particular plant when ill, and prepare the plant in a particular way. They avoid the same plant when well. Young apes watch their mothers do it. This looks like knowledge that is learned and passed on.

For caterpillars and many insects, the taste for bitter leaves when ill is probably inherited, and no learning is needed. For apes there are still only a few clear cases, so more watching is needed before anyone can be sure.

explanations.art: An orangutan with a small wound on his face chewing a green leaf, sitting high in a rainforest tree.

explanations.concept: Protection: stopping a disease before it starts
explanations.context: This card lists the protections against common diseases. Each one blocks a cause, so the disease never begins.
explanations.definition: Prevention means blocking the cause of a disease before the disease starts. It costs less than a cure and spares the person the illness.
explanations.description: Each kind of cause has its own protection. Against germs, the protections are safe drinking water, cooked food, a toilet, hand-washing with soap, mosquito nets, fresh air and vaccines. India's free vaccination programme protects children against about a dozen diseases. Among them are polio, measles, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, tuberculosis and hepatitis B. Smallpox was wiped out across the world by 1980. India had its last case of polio in 2011. Against a missing nutrient, the protections are a varied plate, iodised salt, sunlight, and iron tablets for those a doctor says need them. Against the slow harms of the way we live, the protections are no tobacco, clean air, daily exercise, enough sleep, and not too much sugar, salt and fried food. Against poisoning, medicines and cleaning liquids must be locked away from small children. A check-up can find a disease early, when it is easier to treat. A health worker called an ASHA brings many of these protections to village homes.
examples: A mosquito net costs a few hundred rupees. It blocks the night-biting mosquitoes who carry malaria and filariasis.
Two drops of polio vaccine cost very little. A child paralysed by polio needs care for a whole lifetime.
The iodine in iodised salt costs only a few paise a day, and it prevents goitre.
explanations.art: A row of small pictures: a tap with a filter, a bar of soap, a mosquito net, a vaccine card, a plate of mixed food and a child running.

explanations.context: This card gives the rules for medicines that every family needs. The first rule is for you.
explanations.definition: A medicine is given only by a grown-up, in the way a doctor or the label says. A child never takes, tastes, mixes or shares a medicine alone.
explanations.description: First: only a grown-up gives a medicine. If you find a tablet or a bottle, do not taste it. Take it to a grown-up. Second: the right medicine for the cause. A doctor chooses it, and a chemist may sell an antibiotic only against a prescription. In India a red line on the back of a strip marks such medicines. Third: the right dose at the right times, measured with the cup or the spoon that came with the bottle. A kitchen spoon is not a measure. Fourth: never two doses at once to make up for a missed dose. Fifth: never give one person's medicine to another person. Sixth: check the expiry date, and return old medicines to a chemist. Seventh: keep every medicine in its own packet, locked or high up, away from small children. Nobody should call a medicine a sweet. Eighth: tell the doctor about every medicine, tonic and home remedy the person already takes. If a child swallows a medicine by mistake, a grown-up takes child and packet to a hospital at once. The ambulance number in most of India is 108.
examples: A red vertical line on a tablet strip means that the medicine is sold only with a doctor's prescription.
A syrup is measured in its own cup, because a kitchen teaspoon may hold 3 millilitres or 7.
A grandmother's blood pressure tablets can badly harm a toddler who finds them.
explanations.art: A locked medicine box on a high kitchen shelf, with a measuring cup beside it and a small child far below reaching only as high as the counter.

agreed.text: Most colds end in seven to ten days, whatever remedy is taken.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have followed thousands of people with colds, some given remedies and some given none. The colds lasted about the same time in both. In trials, antibiotics did not shorten a cold either.

agreed.text: A fair trial, with a comparison group chosen by chance, is the reliable way to test a medicine.
agreed.evidence: In 1948, random numbers put 107 patients with tuberculosis into two groups. After six months, 4 of the 55 given streptomycin had died, and 14 of the 52 given bed rest alone.

agreed.text: A deficiency disease is cured by the missing nutrient, and no germ-killing medicine helps.
agreed.evidence: In 1897 Adolphe Vorderman compared the prisons of Java. Where prisoners ate mostly polished white rice, beriberi was common. Where they ate brown rice, it was very rare.

agreed.text: Some medicines replace what the body has lost or cannot make, and they save lives without curing the disease.
agreed.evidence: Before insulin, children with type 1 diabetes died within a year or two. Since 1922, people who inject insulin every day live for many decades. In 1971 Dr Dilip Mahalanabis gave ORS to cholera patients in refugee camps at Bongaon in West Bengal. Deaths fell from about 30 in 100 to under 4 in 100.

agreed.text: The right medicines work as well at home as in a hospital, if they are taken properly.
agreed.evidence: From 1956, a trial in Madras, now Chennai, studied about 190 tuberculosis patients. Chance sent each one to home treatment or to a year in a sanatorium. After a year, the home group had done nearly as well as the sanatorium group.

agreed.text: Vaccines and clean water prevent more illness than medicines cure.
agreed.evidence: Smallpox once killed about three in ten of the people who caught it. Vaccination ended it everywhere by 1980. India has had no case of polio from the wild virus since January 2011.

challenging.claim: I took the remedy and got better, so the remedy worked.
challenging.for: The recovery did come after the remedy, and a person knows how their own body felt.
challenging.against: Most colds, coughs and aches end by themselves. People take remedies on their worst day, after which they improve anyway. Only a comparison with people who took nothing can show what the remedy added.
challenging.context: This is a common way of judging remedies, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: A remedy that has been used for centuries must work.
challenging.who: Many people in every country believe this.
challenging.for: Useless remedies should have been dropped long ago. Some old remedies, such as sarpagandha root, did become medicines.
challenging.against: Bloodletting was used for about two thousand years and did harm. A useless remedy can last for centuries, because most of its patients get better anyway.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about old remedies, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Natural remedies are always safe, because they come from plants.
challenging.for: Many plant foods and spices are safe in kitchen amounts.
challenging.against: Plants make chemicals to defend themselves. Datura seeds and oleander leaves can kill. A plant strong enough to act as a medicine is strong enough to have side effects.
challenging.context: This is a claim found in many advertisements, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: An injection is stronger than a tablet.
challenging.who: Many people in many clinics across India believe this.
challenging.for: An injection acts faster, and a few medicines work only when injected.
challenging.against: For most illnesses the same medicine by mouth works as well. An injection given without need adds pain, cost and a small risk of infection.
challenging.context: This is a common belief about injections, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: A costly branded medicine works better than a cheap generic one.
challenging.who: Many buyers believe this, and so do some sellers.
challenging.for: A known brand may check its quality more carefully, and quality does differ between factories.
challenging.against: The generic and the brand hold the same substance in the same dose. Studies that compared them found the same results in patients. India's Jan Aushadhi shops sell tested generics at much lower prices.
challenging.context: This is a common belief about the price of medicines, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: A dummy tablet can heal real disease, if the patient believes in it.
challenging.who: Some doctors believe this, and many writers do too.
challenging.for: People given a placebo often report less pain and feel better.
challenging.against: When the body is measured, a placebo changes little. In the 2011 asthma trial, people felt better after a dummy inhaler, but their airways had not opened.
challenging.context: This is an idea that scientists still argue about, with the evidence on each side.

big_questions.q: In the Wilted Stems Trial, the stems in plain water stood up again. Who revived the stems: the water, or the stems themselves?
big_questions.hint: Water alone in a glass does not stand up. What did the stems do with the water?

big_questions.q: A doctor stitches a cut, and a week later the skin has joined. Who healed the cut?
big_questions.hint: List what the doctor did and what the skin cells did. Could either have managed alone?

big_questions.q: A person who takes insulin every day is well. Is that person ill or healthy?
big_questions.hint: Think about a person who wears spectacles every day. Does the word 'ill' fit a person who takes insulin, or a person who wears spectacles?

big_questions.q: A dummy inhaler made people feel better, but their breathing was the same. Were they better?
big_questions.hint: Is feeling better part of being better? Who should decide, the patient or the measuring machine?

big_questions.q: In a trial, half the ill people get a dummy. Is that fair to them?
big_questions.hint: Nobody yet knows whether the new medicine helps or harms. If it were never properly tested, what would be unfair to everyone who falls ill later?

big_questions.q: A chimpanzee chews a bitter plant when she is ill. Is that medicine, in the way a tablet is medicine?
big_questions.hint: What makes something a medicine: who made it, or what it does for the one who takes it?

big_questions.q: A new medicine can cost crores of rupees to test. Who should pay, and who should get the medicine?
big_questions.hint: Think about the company, the government and an ill person with little money. India's cheap generic medicines are one answer.

story.title: Across the Stream
story.note: Ponnu, Ajji, Kaveramma, Somanna, Chinni and the estate are made up. These facts are real. Kodagu in Karnataka is a hill district of coffee estates, and its June rains are among the heaviest in India. Streams there rise in hours, and footbridges made of areca logs are sometimes carried away. Kashaya is a hot drink of pepper, dry ginger, tulsi and other herbs, taken for colds across South India. A common cold lasts about seven to ten days with or without any remedy. In a trial in 2007, honey at bedtime eased children's night coughs a little. Honey is never given to a baby under one year. A fever that lasts more than three days, or fast and difficult breathing, needs a doctor.
text: The rain came to Kodagu on the first of June, and by the fourth, half the estate school was coughing.

Ponnu was eleven, and she was not worried. Her grandmother's kashaya was known on every hill around. Ajji roasted pepper and dry ginger, pounded them with tulsi, and boiled the powder black. She stirred a spoon of honey into each tumbler. 'Seven days of my kashaya,' people said, 'and the cold is gone.'
But Ajji had left for a wedding in Mangaluru, and she would be away for twelve days. She had given her jar of powder to Kaveramma, who cooked the noon meal at the school.
'Brew one kettle each morning,' Ajji had said. 'One small tumbler for each child who coughs. Ponnu will carry.'

So on Monday morning Kaveramma brewed, and Ponnu carried. Twenty-three children went to the school. Twelve lived in the upper lines, on Ponnu's side of the stream. Eleven lived in the lower lines, on the far side, and crossed every day on a bridge made of two areca logs.
That Monday every child who coughed drank a tumbler and pulled a face.
On Monday night the stream rose. By morning it was brown and loud, and the two logs were gone.

Ponnu stood on the bank with the kettle in her hand. On the far bank stood Somanna, who sat beside her in class, and his small sister Chinni. The water was too loud for shouting. Chinni coughed, and Ponnu saw her shoulders shake, though she heard nothing.
'Nobody crosses until the water falls,' said Kaveramma. 'Not you, not the kettle. Come away.'

Every morning that week, the twelve children of the upper lines drank their kashaya. Every night Ponnu lay awake and listened to the rain on the tiles. She thought of the eleven on the far bank, coughing with nothing to help them. She counted the days for them on her fingers.
By the next Monday, the coughs on her side had gone. It had taken seven days, as people always said. Only little Muthu still sniffed.

On Wednesday the water fell. The men laid two new logs before noon. Ponnu did not wait for the meal. She filled the kettle to the top and ran across the bridge. The kashaya slopped hot over her wrist.
She had her words ready. I am sorry. We could not come. Drink this now, it is not too late.

In the yard of the lower lines, eleven children were playing lagori. Somanna had just knocked down the seven stones, and he was running, and he was not coughing. Chinni was shouting the score. Nobody was coughing.
'When did it stop?' Ponnu asked. She was still out of breath.
'What?'
'Your cough. All of you.'
Somanna thought. 'Sunday. Monday, for Chinni.' He looked at the kettle. 'Is that for us? We are well now.'

Ponnu walked back over the logs slowly. The kettle was still full. Seven days on this bank, with the kashaya. Seven days on that bank, with nothing. She poured the kettle out under a coffee bush and watched the ground drink it.
Ajji came home on Friday, with wedding sweets wrapped in a banana leaf. Ponnu did not touch them.
'Your kashaya does nothing,' she said. Her voice shook. 'They had none, and they got well on the same day as us. Everyone says seven days of your kashaya. It is seven days of nothing, too.'
She waited for Ajji to be angry. Ajji sat down on the step and untied her bundle.
'How did they sleep?' Ajji asked.
'What?'
'The eleven. In the first nights. Did you ask?'

Ponnu had not asked. So on Saturday the two of them crossed the logs together, and Ajji asked the mothers. The mothers said the first four nights had been bad. The children had coughed until the cocks crowed, and nobody in the lines had slept. On Ponnu's side, the children had drunk the warm tumbler and slept.

'I never said my kashaya sends a cold away,' said Ajji, on the way home. 'People said that. A cold goes when the body has finished with it. The body takes about seven days, and I cannot make it six. I only make the nights softer.'
'Then why does everyone say it cures?'

'Because they drink, and afterwards they are well. They tie the two together. Nobody ever saw what you saw.' Ajji stopped on the bridge and looked down at the water. 'I have brewed for thirty years, child, and I never had two banks. The stream gave you one bank with the kashaya and one bank without. That is the only way to know what a remedy adds.'
They walked on. 'And one more thing,' said Ajji. 'When Kaveramma's boy had a fever for five days, and his chest pulled in at every breath, did I brew for him?'
Ponnu remembered. 'You sent for the jeep. They took him to the hospital in Madikeri.'

'A cold is a waiting illness. His was not. The body could not finish that one alone, and the doctor had the medicine that would help. A healer must know which is which. That matters more than any powder.'
On Monday, Chinni caught a new cold from somebody. Ajji brewed that evening, and Ponnu carried a tumbler across the logs.
'This will not make your cold go faster,' she told Chinni. 'It will take seven days anyway. This is for tonight, so that you sleep.'
Chinni drank it and pulled a face.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Ponnu believed what everyone said, that seven days of kashaya cures a cold. The flooded stream made a comparison by accident. One group of children drank the kashaya and one group had none. Both were well in the same seven days. So the kashaya did not shorten the cold. The body ended the cold. What the remedy added could be found only by comparing the two banks: it eased the nights. Ajji also names the limit of home remedies. Some illnesses do not end by themselves, and those need a doctor.
ask: A cold ended seven days after a remedy. What else do you need to know before you say that the remedy worked?
Why can a comparison show something that thirty years of careful practice did not show?
A remedy does not shorten an illness, but it helps a child sleep. Is that remedy worth taking? Why?
How can a family tell an illness that needs waiting from an illness that needs a doctor?
