games.title: Find the Cause: the clinic card game
games.context: This is a card game about causes. Each card gives the clues of a made-up patient. You decide which of five kinds of cause is at work, and what kind of help fits that cause.

printables.title: 16 patient cards: clues on the front, the cause and the help on the back. Print on both sides

items.f: Watery loose motions many times a day, after drinking from a roadside tap. A dry mouth and great thirst.
items.b: GERM, in dirty water. Help: ORS at once, to replace the lost water and salts, and a doctor. Safe water prevents it.

items.f: Fever with shivering every second day, after many mosquito bites.
items.b: GERM: the malaria parasite, carried by a mosquito. Help: a blood test, and the antimalarial medicine a doctor orders. A net prevents it.

items.f: A fever that climbs higher each day for a week, with stomach pain. The person ate cut fruit from an uncovered cart.
items.b: GERM: the typhoid bacterium, in food or water. Help: a blood test, and an antibiotic chosen by a doctor. Safe food and a vaccine prevent it.

items.f: A cough for more than three weeks, loss of weight and a fever every evening.
items.b: GERM: the tuberculosis bacterium, in the air. Help: a spit test, and six months of medicines. Fresh air and good food help prevent it.

items.f: A sudden high fever with pain behind the eyes and in the joints, in the rainy season. Water stands in old tyres nearby.
items.b: GERM: the dengue virus, carried by a day-biting mosquito. Help: no medicine kills this virus. Rest, plenty to drink, and a doctor to watch the blood. Emptying standing water prevents it.

items.f: A runny nose, sneezing and a mild sore throat for three days.
items.b: GERM: a cold virus. Help: no medicine removes the virus. Rest and warm drinks. The body clears it in about a week.

items.f: A woman is pale, tired and out of breath. Her meals are mostly rice and tea.
items.b: MISSING NUTRIENT: iron. This is anaemia. Help: ragi, chana and greens with lemon, and iron tablets if a doctor says so.

items.f: A child sees well at noon but bumps into things at dusk.
items.b: MISSING NUTRIENT: vitamin A. This is night blindness. Help: drumstick leaves, carrot, papaya and mango. A health worker may give a vitamin A dose.

items.f: A small child's legs are bowed. He lives in a dark lane and is rarely out in the sun.
items.b: MISSING NUTRIENT: vitamin D, or calcium. This is rickets. Help: sunlight, milk, curd and ragi, and a doctor's advice.

items.f: A swelling at the front of the neck, in a village where the salt is not iodised.
items.b: MISSING NUTRIENT: iodine. This is goitre. Help: iodised salt. It also prevents goitre for the whole village.

items.f: Bleeding gums, and old cuts that open again. No fruit or vegetables for many months.
items.b: MISSING NUTRIENT: vitamin C. This is scurvy. Help: amla, guava, lemon and fresh vegetables. Recovery starts within days.

items.f: A girl of nine is very thirsty and is losing weight, though she eats well. A test shows very high sugar in her blood.
items.b: A BODY PART HAS STOPPED WORKING: her pancreas no longer makes insulin. This is type 1 diabetes. Help: insulin injections every day, which replace what the pancreas made.

items.f: A grandmother's sight has grown misty in both eyes, slowly, over two years.
items.b: A BODY PART HAS STOPPED WORKING WELL: the lens of each eye has clouded. This is cataract. Help: a short operation puts in a new clear lens. No medicine clears a cataract.

items.f: A man of 50 has smoked for thirty years. He coughs every morning and is breathless on the stairs.
items.b: HARM FROM OUTSIDE: tobacco smoke has damaged his lungs. Help: stopping smoking, and inhalers to ease the breathing. The damage cannot be undone.

items.f: A man of 45 sits all day and eats many fried snacks and sweets. He feels well, but a test shows high sugar in his blood.
items.b: THE WAY OF LIFE, often with a family tendency. This is type 2 diabetes. Help: changes in food, a daily walk, and the tablets a doctor orders.

items.f: A child has had bouts of severe bone pain and anaemia since she was a baby. An uncle and a cousin have the same illness.
items.b: AN INHERITED FAULT: sickle cell disease, passed down in the genes. Nobody catches it. Help: lifelong care and medicines from a doctor. A blood test can find it at birth.

printables.title: 5 cause mats: write each on a sheet of paper
items: A BODY PART HAS STOPPED WORKING WELL
HARM FROM OUTSIDE, OR THE WAY OF LIFE

rules: Lay the five cause mats in a row. Shuffle the 16 patient cards and put them in a pile, clues side up.
On your turn, take the top card and read the clues aloud. Do not look at the back.
Put the card on the cause mat you choose. Then say what kind of help fits.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. Score 1 point for the right mat, and 1 point if your help matches.
A wrong card goes to the bottom of the pile to be played again.
The game ends when every card is on its right mat. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Sort all 16 cards on to the mats first. Then turn them over and count how many you placed correctly. Shuffle and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Five sheets of paper in a row on a table, each with a cause written in capitals, and a pile of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the five cause mats. Put the 16 patient cards in a pile, clues side up.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud and holding it above one of five paper mats.
setup.caption: 2. Read the clues. Put the card on a cause mat, and say what would help.

setup.art: A card turned over on the table showing its back, with another player pointing at the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for the cause and a point for the help.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards and write the five mats. 2. Read the five mats aloud. 3. Play one card together as practice.
flow.say: Each card is a made-up patient. First we find the kind of cause. Then we say what help fits that cause.
flow.kid: Lay out five mats. Shuffle the cards. Play one card together to practise.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Cause. You lay out the mats and practise with one card.

flow.do: Play by the rules until every card is on its right mat. After each card, ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the clues aloud. Which mat? What help fits? Now turn the card over. Which clue should have told you?
flow.kid: Take a card. Read the clues. Choose a mat. Say what helps. Turn it over.

ask.q: Which clue pointed to the cause?
good: The mosquito bites pointed to malaria.
Eating no fruit for months pointed to a missing vitamin.
The uncle and cousin with the same illness pointed to an inherited fault.

flow.parent: Some real diseases belong on two mats. Type 2 diabetes is partly inherited and partly the way of life. Accept a second mat if your child gives a good reason.
flow.context: In this step of Find the Cause you play the patient cards, choosing a cause and a help for each.

flow.do: Count the points. Spread the cards on their mats, backs up. Ask how many of the 16 patients are helped by a medicine that kills a germ.
flow.say: Look at the backs of all sixteen cards. For how many patients is the help a medicine that kills a germ? What helps the others?
flow.kid: Count your points. How many patients need a germ-killing medicine? What helps the rest?

check.q: A person has scurvy, caused by too little vitamin C. Which help fits the cause?
options: Fruit and vegetables with vitamin C
An antibiotic
A medicine for pain
check.why: Scurvy has no germ, so an antibiotic has nothing to kill. A pain medicine would hide a symptom and leave the cause. Only the missing vitamin removes the cause. Of the 16 patients, only three need a germ-killing medicine: malaria, typhoid and tuberculosis.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Cause. You count how many patients are helped by a germ-killing medicine, and what helps the others.

games.title: Tale, Hint or Trial? How strong is the evidence?
games.context: This is a card game about evidence. Each card says how somebody 'knows' that a remedy works. You decide whether it is a tale that shows little, a hint worth testing, or a fair trial.

printables.title: 18 evidence cards: the claim on the front, the answer on the back. Print on both sides

items.f: My aunt drank ginger tea, and her cold was gone in a week.
items.b: TALE. A cold is gone in a week anyway. This is one person, with nobody to compare.

items.f: A film star says in an advertisement that a tonic keeps her healthy.
items.b: TALE. She is one person, and she is paid to say it. There is no comparison.

items.f: This remedy has been used for 500 years.
items.b: TALE. Age is not evidence. Bloodletting was used for 2,000 years and did harm.

items.f: A phone message says that a fruit cures diabetes. It has been forwarded many times.
items.b: TALE. Forwarding is not evidence. The message gives no names, no counts and no comparison.

items.f: On a shop's website, nine of ten buyers of a balm say that it helped.
items.b: TALE. People who were not helped seldom write. Nobody counted the buyers who stayed silent, or people who used nothing.

items.f: A man took a powder on the worst day of his fever and felt better the next morning.
items.b: TALE. After the worst day, most fevers improve anyway.

items.f: A doctor gave a new syrup to 20 patients, and all 20 recovered. She had no second group.
items.b: HINT. Twenty counted patients are better than one story. But they might all have recovered anyway. It is worth a fair trial.

items.f: In villages that eat brown rice, beriberi is rare. In villages that eat polished rice, beriberi is common.
items.b: HINT. This is a pattern across many people. But the villages may differ in other ways too. The test is to change the rice and count again.

items.f: In a laboratory, a plant juice kills malaria parasites in a glass dish.
items.b: HINT. A dish is not a body. Many substances kill germs in a dish and then fail, or do harm, inside a person.

items.f: A chimpanzee with a stomach illness chewed a bitter plant and was well the next day.
items.b: HINT. This is one case, with no comparison. It is a good reason to study the plant.

items.f: Fifty patients took a new tablet and fifty took nothing. The doctor chose who got the tablet. The tablet group did better.
items.b: HINT. There is a comparison, but chance did not choose the groups. The doctor may have picked the stronger patients for the tablet without meaning to.

items.f: A new medicine cured an illness in mice.
items.b: HINT. Mice are not people. Many medicines that work in mice fail in humans.

items.f: Four hundred people were put into two groups by chance. One group got a tablet and the other a dummy that looked the same. Nobody knew which until the end. The tablet group recovered two days sooner.
items.b: TRIAL. There were two groups, and chance chose who went into each one. One group got a dummy, nobody knew who got what, and many people took part. This is strong evidence.

items.f: In 1948, random numbers put 107 patients with tuberculosis into two groups. Of 55 given a new medicine, 4 died. Of 52 given bed rest alone, 14 died.
items.b: TRIAL. This was the first fair trial of its kind. The groups were chosen by chance and then counted.

items.f: In a trial, 6,799 babies were given a vaccine or a dummy, by chance. Severe diarrhoea was about half as common in the vaccine group.
items.b: TRIAL. Chance chose who got the vaccine, the other babies got a dummy, and thousands of babies took part. This trial tested India's Rotavac vaccine.

items.f: Three separate fair trials, in three countries, all found that a medicine lowered blood pressure.
items.b: TRIAL. A result that is repeated by different teams is the strongest evidence of all.

items.f: A fair, blind trial of 300 children found that an antibiotic did not shorten their colds.
items.b: TRIAL. A fair trial can also show that something does not work. That is just as useful.

items.f: Twelve wilted stems were put by coin toss into sugar water or plain water. The person who counted did not know which glass was which.
items.b: TRIAL. The design is fair: two groups, chance and blind counting. But twelve stems are few, so it should be repeated.

printables.title: 3 mats: write each on a sheet of paper

rules: Lay the three mats in a row. Shuffle the 18 cards and put them in a pile, claim side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Put it on TALE, HINT or TRIAL.
Say what is missing: a comparison group, chance, a dummy, blind counting or enough people. If nothing is missing, say so.
Turn the card over and read the back. Score 1 point for the right mat, and 1 more if you named what was missing.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Sort all 18 cards, then turn them over and check. There are six for each mat. Shuffle and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper in a row marked TALE, HINT and TRIAL, with a pile of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats. Put the 18 cards in a pile, claim side up.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud and placing it on the middle sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Read the claim. Put it on TALE, HINT or TRIAL, and say what is missing.

setup.art: A card turned over to show its back, with two players leaning in to read it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for the mat and a point for what was missing.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards and write the three mats. 2. Say the five things a fair trial needs: two groups, chance, a dummy, blind counting and many people. 3. Play one card together.
flow.say: Each card says how somebody knows that a remedy works. A tale shows very little. A hint is worth testing. A trial is strong evidence.
flow.kid: Lay out three mats. Say the five things a fair trial needs. Play one card together.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tale, Hint or Trial. You lay out the mats and recall what a fair trial needs.

flow.do: Play by the rules until the pile is finished. After each card, ask what is missing.
flow.say: Read the claim aloud. Tale, hint or trial? What is missing from it? Now turn it over.
flow.kid: Read a card. Choose a mat. Say what is missing. Turn it over.

ask.q: What is missing from this claim?
good: There is no group of people who took nothing, so there is nothing to compare with.
Chance did not choose the groups.
There is only one person.

flow.parent: A tale is not a lie. The aunt really did get well. A tale simply cannot show what caused the recovery.
flow.context: In this step of Tale, Hint or Trial you sort each claim by how strong its evidence is.

flow.do: Count the points. Lay the six TALE cards in a row, and ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the six tales. They are the kind of evidence we hear every day. Why are they so easy to believe?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the six tales. Why are tales easy to believe?

check.q: Which is the strongest evidence that a cough syrup works?
options: Two groups by chance, one given a dummy
Twenty people who all got better
A doctor who has used it for years
check.why: Coughs usually end by themselves. So twenty recoveries, or years of use, cannot show what the syrup added. Only a second group, chosen by chance and given a dummy, shows what would have happened without the syrup.

flow.context: This is the last step of Tale, Hint or Trial. You think about why weak evidence is easy to believe.

experiments.title: The Half-Glass Test: does a medicine keep building up when dose follows dose?
experiments.context: In this experiment a glass of water stands for a body. Spoons of black tea stand for doses of a medicine. Pouring away half the glass stands for the liver and kidneys removing the medicine. You find out what happens to the level when dose follows dose. No real medicine is used.
experiments.question: A body removes half of a medicine every few hours. A new dose is given each time. Does the amount in the body keep rising, dose after dose? Or does it stop rising?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Each dose is 2 teaspoons of tea. Before each new dose, half the glass is poured away and replaced with water. After six doses, how much tea will be in the glass: about 4 teaspoons, about 8, or about 12? Will the glass be darker than the TWO DOSES glass? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same glass for the body every time, with the same FULL line and HALF line. Use level teaspoons of the same tea. Pour away exactly to the HALF line, add the dose, and fill with water exactly to the FULL line. Stir before you compare. Compare colours side by side on white paper, in the same light. Only one thing changes: how many doses have gone in.
results_table: Teaspoons of tea in the glass just before the dose
Teaspoons of tea in the glass just after the dose
Colour after the dose, against the three colour glasses

materials.item: clear glasses of the same size and shape. Clear plastic cups, or the bottoms of clear bottles cut by a grown-up, also work
strong black tea without milk, cooled: about 1 and a half cups. Or 10 drops of food colour stirred into 1 and a half cups of water
drinking water, about 2 litres, in a jug
a teaspoon, and a tea cup for measuring
a marker pen, or strips of tape, for the two lines
a sheet of white paper, and a bowl or bucket for the poured-away water
four paper slips for labels: BODY, LOW, ONE DOSE, TWO DOSES

experiments.safety: The tea is a pretend medicine, and no real medicine is used. A grown-up boils and strains the tea, and cuts any bottles. Nobody drinks from the test glasses.

schedule.what: Make three colour glasses. Then add dose after dose of tea to the BODY glass, pouring half away each time, and track the level.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each dose. Write the teaspoons of tea in the glass before and after each dose, as worked out by halving. Beside each, write which colour glass the BODY glass matches.

example_chart.title: The amounts worked out by halving (your colours should follow them)
rows: between ONE DOSE and TWO DOSES
almost TWO DOSES, and no darker

setup.art: Four identical clear glasses on white paper, three holding tea water in pale, medium and dark shades with slips reading LOW, ONE DOSE and TWO DOSES, and one glass of plain water labelled BODY.
setup.caption: 1. Make three colour glasses with 1, 2 and 4 teaspoons of tea. Fill the BODY glass with water. Mark a FULL line and a HALF line.

setup.art: A child adding a level teaspoon of dark tea to a glass of water marked with two lines.
setup.caption: 2. A dose is 2 teaspoons of tea. Add one dose to the BODY glass and stir.

setup.art: A child pouring water from the marked glass into a bowl until the water sits at the lower line.
setup.caption: 3. Pour away down to the HALF line. This is the liver and kidneys removing half.

setup.art: A child adding two teaspoons of tea to the half-full glass, then topping up from a jug to the upper line.
setup.caption: 4. Add the next dose and fill to the FULL line with water. Compare the colour. Repeat for six doses.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils 2 heaped teaspoons of tea leaves in 2 cups of water for 3 minutes. They strain the tea and cool it. 2. Pour 1 tea cup of water into the BODY glass. Mark the water level with the pen. This is the FULL line. 3. Pour from the BODY glass into an empty matching glass until the two levels are equal. Mark this level on the BODY glass. This is the HALF line. Pour the water back. 4. Pour 1 tea cup of water into each of the other three glasses. 5. Stir 1 teaspoon of tea into the LOW glass, 2 into ONE DOSE and 4 into TWO DOSES.
flow.say: This glass of water is a pretend body, and the tea is a pretend medicine. The three colour glasses show one, two and four teaspoons of tea. We will compare the BODY glass with them.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes strong tea. Mark FULL and HALF on the BODY glass. Make three colour glasses.
flow.parent: The tea should be dark. One teaspoon in a cup of water must still show a pale colour against white paper. If the LOW glass looks like plain water, boil the tea longer or use 2 teaspoons as the unit throughout.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Half-Glass Test. You make the pretend medicine, mark the BODY glass and make three colour glasses to compare with.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the plan: one dose is 2 teaspoons, and half the glass is poured away before every new dose. 2. Ask for the guess and the reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: A body removes half of a medicine every few hours. Then the next dose arrives. After six doses, how much tea will be in the glass? Will it be darker than TWO DOSES? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six doses will go in. Half is poured away each time. How much tea stays? Why?

ask.q: Six doses of 2 teaspoons make 12 teaspoons. Will all 12 be in the glass at the end?
good: No, some is poured away each time.
I think half of it will go.
I think most of it stays, because we keep adding.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the glass to grow darker without limit.
flow.context: In this step of the Half-Glass Test you guess how much tea the glass will hold after six doses.

flow.do: 1. Add one dose, 2 teaspoons, to the BODY glass and stir. Compare with ONE DOSE. 2. Pour away to the HALF line and fill to FULL with water. Compare with LOW. 3. Do this twice more, with no new dose. 4. Write the teaspoons left each time: 2, then 1, then a half, then a quarter.
flow.say: First we give one dose only. Then we pour half away three times. Watch the colour against the LOW glass. How long does one dose last?
flow.kid: Add one dose. Pour half away and refill. Do it three times. Watch the colour fade.

ask.q: After which pour was the BODY glass paler than the LOW glass?
good: After the second pour.
After two pours only half a teaspoon was left.

flow.parent: After one pour the glass matches LOW. After two it is paler. Say that LOW stands for the smallest amount that still works. One dose falls below it, so another dose is needed. Rinse the BODY glass and fill it with fresh water to FULL.
flow.context: In this step of the Half-Glass Test you give one dose only. You watch the colour fade as half is poured away each time.

flow.do: 1. Add dose 1 and stir. Write 2 teaspoons. 2. Pour away to HALF. Add dose 2. Fill to FULL and stir. 3. Work out the tea now in the glass: half of 2 is 1, and 1 plus 2 is 3. Write it. 4. Compare the colour with the three colour glasses. 5. Repeat until six doses have gone in.
flow.say: Now a dose goes in every time. Before each dose, half is poured away. Work out the teaspoons each time, then check the colour. Is it still getting darker?
flow.kid: Add a dose. Pour to HALF. Add the next dose and refill. Work out the teaspoons. Do six doses.
flow.parent: The amounts go 2, 3, 3 and a half, 3 and three-quarters, and then just under 4. The colour comes close to TWO DOSES by the third or fourth dose, and then stops changing. Then empty and rinse the BODY glass.

check.q: In the Half-Glass Test, the glass holds 3 teaspoons of tea. Half is poured away and a dose of 2 is added. How much tea is in the glass now?
options: 3 and a half teaspoons
5 teaspoons
2 and a half teaspoons
check.why: Half of 3 is 1 and a half. Adding the dose of 2 makes 3 and a half. If you chose 5, you added the dose but forgot the pour. If you chose 2 and a half, you halved the dose as well as the tea in the glass.

flow.context: In this step of the Half-Glass Test you add six doses, pouring half away before each one. You track the amount of tea.

flow.do: 1. Fill the rinsed BODY glass with water to the FULL line. 2. This time each dose is 4 teaspoons. Do three doses, pouring to HALF before each. 3. Work out the teaspoons: 4, then 6, then 7. 4. Compare the colour with the TWO DOSES glass, which the six single doses never passed.
flow.say: Suppose someone takes two doses at once, every time, to get well faster. Work out the teaspoons, and compare with the TWO DOSES glass. What happened to the level?
flow.kid: Now each dose is 4 teaspoons. Do three doses. Compare with the TWO DOSES glass.

ask.q: The single doses stopped rising near 4 teaspoons. Where will the double doses stop?
good: Near 8 teaspoons.
Twice as high, because every dose is twice as big.

flow.parent: After three double doses the glass holds 7 teaspoons and is clearly darker than TWO DOSES. If TWO DOSES stood for the highest safe level, this body is now above it.
flow.context: In this step of the Half-Glass Test you double every dose, and compare the glass with the TWO DOSES glass.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Why did the level stop near 4 teaspoons?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the tea stop rising near 4 teaspoons?
good: When the glass holds 4 teaspoons, each pour removes 2 teaspoons, and each dose adds 2 teaspoons.
The more tea in the glass, the more each pour takes away.

ask.q: What does this tell you about taking two doses at once after a missed dose?
good: The level goes higher than it was meant to go.
It could go above the safe level, so a grown-up asks the doctor instead.

flow.parent: The reason: each pour removes half of whatever is there. A fuller glass loses more. When the glass holds about 4 teaspoons, the pour removes 2 and the dose adds 2, so the level stays. A body treats most medicines this way. The makers choose the dose and the gap so that the level stays between too little and too much. Real bodies remove medicines little by little, and the pour does it all at once. So the glass is a model.
flow.think: A medicine label says 'every 8 hours'. What might happen to the level if the doses were taken every 4 hours instead?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Half-Glass Test. You say what your numbers show about how a medicine builds up in a body.

experiments.title: The Wilted Stems Trial: does sugar in the water revive limp coriander?
experiments.context: In this experiment you run a fair trial, the way doctors test a medicine. Some people say a spoon of sugar in the water revives wilted greens. You give limp coriander stems sugar water or plain water, chosen by a coin. Then you count how many stand up again.
experiments.question: Do limp coriander stems recover better in sugar water than in plain water? And what would you have thought if you had tried only the sugar water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Six limp stems go into sugar water, six into plain water, and three stay on a dry plate. After two hours, how many in each group will stand up again? Which group will do best? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the stems come from the same bunch and wilt on the same plate for the same time. A coin decides which glass each stem joins, so nobody can pick the fresher stems for one glass. Both glasses hold 1 cup of water and stand side by side. The person who counts does not know which glass has the sugar. Only one thing differs between the glasses: the sugar.
results_table: Glass A: stems recovered, out of 6
Glass B: stems recovered, out of 6
Dry plate: stems recovered, out of 3

materials.item: fresh coriander stems with their leaves, each about as long as your hand. Mint, methi, palak or keerai also work
glasses or steel tumblers of the same size
drinking water, 2 cups
sugar, 1 level teaspoon
a coin, a plate, scissors and a clock
two paper slips marked A and B, and a folded slip for the grown-up's secret note

experiments.safety: Use scissors with care. The stems are food: rinse them afterwards and use them in tonight's cooking.

schedule.what: Let 15 coriander stems wilt for 2 to 3 hours. Put them by coin toss into sugar water or plain water. Count the recovered stems after 30 minutes, 1 hour and 2 hours.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each time: start, 30 minutes, 1 hour and 2 hours. Write how many stems have recovered in glass A, in glass B and on the dry plate.

setup.art: Fifteen coriander stems lying limp on a steel plate in a warm kitchen, their leaves drooping.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 15 coriander stems on a plate for 2 to 3 hours, until they are limp but still green.

setup.art: A grown-up, with her back turned to a child, stirring a spoon of sugar into one of two identical glasses of water that stand on slips marked A and B.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up secretly stirs 1 teaspoon of sugar into one glass, and writes down which.

setup.art: A child tossing a coin beside a plate of limp stems, with two glasses each holding a few stems.
setup.caption: 3. Toss a coin for each stem: heads to glass A, tails to glass B. Six in each. Three stay on the plate.

setup.art: A child lifting one coriander stem out of a glass by its lower end and holding it upright to see whether the top stays up.
setup.caption: 4. After 30 minutes, 1 hour and 2 hours, count the stems in each glass that hold their tops up.

flow.do: 1. Take 15 coriander stems of about the same length, with their leaves. 2. Lay them apart on a plate. 3. Leave the plate in a warm room, out of the sun, for 2 to 3 hours.
flow.say: These coriander stems are fresh now. We will leave them without water until they go limp. Later we will test a way of reviving them.
flow.kid: Lay fifteen coriander stems on a plate. Leave them until they are limp.
flow.parent: The stems are ready when they hang down from your fingers but are still green and soft. In a hot, dry room this may take one hour. If the leaves have turned dry and crisp, they have gone too far, so start again with a shorter time.
flow.wait: Leave the stems for 2 to 3 hours, until they are limp
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wilted Stems Trial. You leave coriander stems out of water until they wilt.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the claim: a spoon of sugar in the water revives wilted greens. 2. Ask the first question below, and wait for the answer. 3. Then ask for the guess about three groups, with the reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Some people say sugar in the water revives wilted greens. Suppose we put every stem in sugar water, and they all stand up. Would that show that the sugar works? What else would we need?
flow.kid: People say sugar water revives limp greens. How could you test that fairly? Guess the result. Why?

ask.q: If all the stems in sugar water stand up, why is that not enough?
good: They might stand up in plain water too.
We need some stems without sugar to compare.
Maybe the water did it and the sugar did nothing.

flow.parent: Let your child reach the idea of a second glass by themselves if they can. Do not say what you expect to happen.
flow.context: In this step of the Wilted Stems Trial you plan a fair test of a claim. You guess the result before you try.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 cup of water into each glass and stand them on the slips A and B. 2. Your child looks away. Stir 1 level teaspoon of sugar into one glass until it has dissolved. Write which glass on the folded slip. 3. Your child keeps 3 stems on the plate. 4. They cut a fingernail's width off the bottom of the other 12. 5. They toss a coin for each stem: heads goes to A, tails to B. When one glass has 6, the rest go to the other.
flow.say: I will put sugar in one glass while you look away. Then you toss a coin for each stem. Why should a coin choose, and not you? Why should you not know which glass has the sugar?
flow.kid: Look away while the sugar goes in. Toss a coin for each stem. Six in each glass.

ask.q: Why does a coin choose the glass for each stem?
good: So I cannot put the better stems in one glass.
Chance is fair to both glasses.

ask.q: Why should the person counting not know which glass has the sugar?
good: They might count more kindly for the glass they expect to win.

flow.parent: A fresh cut helps the stem take up water. Stand the glasses side by side, away from the sun, the stove and the fan.
flow.context: In this step of the Wilted Stems Trial a coin puts six limp stems into each glass. You do not know which glass holds the sugar.

flow.do: 1. After 30 minutes, lift each stem out by the bottom end and hold the stem upright. 2. If the top stays up or out, count the stem as recovered. If the top hangs down, count it as limp. 3. Put the stem back in the same glass. 4. Write the count for A, for B and for the plate. 5. Do the same after 1 hour.
flow.say: Hold each stem upright by the bottom end. Does the top stay up, or hang down? Count the recovered stems in each glass, and on the plate.
flow.kid: Hold each stem upright. Does the top stay up? Count for A, B and the plate.
flow.parent: Use the same rule for every stem. If you are unsure about a stem, count it as limp in both glasses.
flow.wait: Count after 30 minutes and again after 1 hour
flow.context: In this step of the Wilted Stems Trial you count the stems that hold their tops up. You count after 30 minutes and after 1 hour.

flow.do: 1. After 2 hours, count all three groups once more. 2. Now open the folded slip and read out which glass had the sugar. 3. Write 'sugar water' and 'plain water' at the top of the right columns.
flow.say: This is the last count. Now I will open the slip. Which glass do you think had the sugar? Why?
flow.kid: Count once more after two hours. Then open the secret slip.

check.q: In the Wilted Stems Trial, which group shows what happens with no sugar?
options: The stems in plain water
The stems on the dry plate
The stems in sugar water
check.why: The plain water glass differs from the sugar glass in one thing only, the sugar. So it is the control group for the sugar. The dry plate has no sugar, but it has no water either, so two things differ. It shows that the stems need water to recover.

flow.wait: Do this 2 hours after the stems went into the glasses
flow.context: In this step of the Wilted Stems Trial you make the last count. Then you find out which glass held the sugar.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. What did the sugar add?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Suppose you had only the sugar glass. What would you have believed?
good: That sugar revives wilted stems.
I would have given the sugar the credit.

ask.q: What did the stems on the dry plate show?
good: Stems do not recover without water.
The water was what the stems needed.

ask.q: How is this like a cold and a remedy?
good: A cold ends anyway, so the remedy gets credit it has not earned.
You need people who took nothing, to compare.

flow.parent: In most kitchens, both glasses recover about equally and the plate stems stay limp. Write what you really found. If one glass did better by a stem or two, that can be luck with only six stems. Run the trial again before you believe it. The reason: a limp stem's cells have lost water. In the glass, water moves up the stem and refills the cells, and the stem stiffens. The stems do this with plain water. One teaspoon of sugar in a cup adds nothing they can use quickly. If fewer than half the stems recovered in both glasses, they were too dry. Try again with a shorter wilting time, or leave them overnight.
flow.think: A coin sent each stem to a glass. In a medicine trial, what does chance decide, and why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Wilted Stems Trial. You say what your counts show about the sugar, and about why a trial needs a comparison group.

experiments.title: The Label Test: does a label change how sweet a drink tastes?
experiments.context: In this experiment you give people two cups of exactly the same lemon drink. One cup is labelled ORDINARY and the other EXTRA SWEET. You find out whether the label changes the scores they give. It shows why a medicine trial must be blind.
experiments.question: Two cups hold the same drink. Do tasters score the cup labelled EXTRA SWEET as sweeter? What do they score when the cups have no labels?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In round 1 the two cups have labels. In round 2 they have none. Will the tasters give the EXTRA SWEET cup a higher score in round 1? Will the two cups score the same in round 2? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Make one jug of the drink and stir it well, so that every cup holds the same drink. Give every taster the same small amount, in the same kind of cup. Each taster scores alone and does not hear the others. Say the same words to each taster. Only one thing changes between the rounds: the labels.

materials.item: drinking water, 3 cups
sugar, 3 level teaspoons, and half a lemon
a jug and a spoon
small cups or steel tumblers, four for serving and one for each taster
two paper labels, ORDINARY and EXTRA SWEET, and a pen for the dots
tasters: at least 4 people from your family or your building. Six or more is better
small slips of paper for the scores

experiments.safety: Wash your hands before you make the drink. Each taster drinks from their own cup. Afterwards, tell every taster the truth about the two cups.

schedule.what: Make one jug of lemon drink. Serve it from two labelled cups, then from two unlabelled cups, and collect each taster's scores.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each taster and four columns of scores. Add up each column. Write the difference between the two cups in round 1, and in round 2.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from four tasters (scores from 1 to 5)

setup.art: A child stirring sugar and lemon juice into a jug of water on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Make one jug of lemon drink: 3 cups of water, 3 teaspoons of sugar and the juice of half a lemon.

setup.art: Two steel serving cups filled from the same jug, one with a paper label ORDINARY and one with a paper label EXTRA SWEET.
setup.caption: 2. Fill two serving cups from the same jug. Label one ORDINARY and one EXTRA SWEET.

setup.art: A grandmother sipping from a small cup and writing a number on a slip of paper, with the two labelled cups in front of her.
setup.caption: 3. Round 1: each taster sips from both and scores the sweetness from 1 to 5.

setup.art: Two plain cups with one dot and two dots drawn underneath, and a child holding a table of scores.
setup.caption: 4. Round 2: the same drink in cups marked only by dots underneath. Collect the scores again.

flow.do: 1. Your child stirs 3 level teaspoons of sugar and the juice of half a lemon into 3 cups of water. 2. They fill two serving cups from the jug and label them ORDINARY and EXTRA SWEET. 3. They fill two more cups, and mark one dot under one and two dots under the other. 4. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: All four cups hold the same drink from one jug. Two have labels, and two have only dots underneath. Will the labels change the scores? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make one jug of lemon drink. Fill four cups. Label two. Guess what the tasters will say.

ask.q: The drinks are the same. So why might the scores differ?
good: People may taste what they expect to taste.
The label tells them it is sweeter, so they believe it.
I think they will not differ, because tongues do not read.

flow.parent: Do not say what you expect. Your child is the tester and knows the secret, so they cannot also be a taster.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Label Test. You make one drink, pour it into labelled and unlabelled cups, and guess what tasters will say.

flow.do: 1. Call one taster at a time. 2. Pour a little from the ORDINARY cup into their cup. They sip and write a sweetness score from 1 to 5 on a slip. 3. Do the same from the EXTRA SWEET cup. 4. Collect the slip. Write the two scores in the table.
flow.say: Please taste these two drinks, one after the other. Score how sweet each one is, from 1 for hardly sweet to 5 for very sweet. Please do not tell anyone your scores.
flow.kid: Call one taster at a time. They sip both drinks. They write a score for each.
flow.parent: Your child must keep a plain face and say the same words to everyone. Tasters should not hear each other's scores.
flow.context: In this step of the Label Test each taster scores two labelled cups, which secretly hold the same drink.

flow.do: 1. When every taster has done round 1, start round 2. 2. Call each taster again. Pour from the one-dot cup, then from the two-dot cup. 3. They score each from 1 to 5. 4. Write the scores in the table.
flow.say: Here are two more drinks. These have no names. Please score how sweet each one is, from 1 to 5.
flow.kid: Now serve from the two cups with dots. No labels this time. Collect the scores.

check.q: In the Label Test, why is round 2 called a blind test?
options: The tasters cannot tell which cup is which
The tasters close their eyes
The tester does not know the scores
check.why: Blind means the people being tested have no clue about which treatment they got. Nobody's eyes are shut. With no labels, only the drink itself can change the score. If you chose the third answer, remember that the tester writes down every score.

flow.context: In this step of the Label Test the same tasters score two unlabelled cups of the same drink. This is the blind round.

flow.do: 1. Add up each of the four columns. 2. Find the difference between the two cups in round 1, and in round 2. 3. Tell every taster kindly that all the cups held the same drink. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Add up each column. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Then let us tell the tasters the truth.
flow.kid: Add up the columns. Say what you thought, what you saw and why. Tell the tasters the truth.

ask.q: What did the label change, the drink or the taster?
good: The taster. The drink was the same.
What they expected changed what they tasted.

ask.q: A patient knows that she got the new medicine and not the dummy. How might that change what she tells the doctor?
good: She may say she feels better because she expects to.
So trials hide who got which.

flow.parent: In many homes the EXTRA SWEET cup scores higher in round 1. The two cups then score about the same in round 2. In some homes the label makes no difference. Write what you really found. With four tasters, a difference of one or two points can be luck, so add more tasters if you can. The reason: the brain builds a taste from the tongue's signal and from what it expects. The same happens with pain and with feeling ill. This is why a medicine trial gives one group a dummy that looks the same, and hides who got which. Nobody was foolish. Everyone's brain works this way.
flow.think: Your tasters were honest, and yet the label may have changed their scores. Can a person always trust what they feel?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Label Test. You compare the labelled round with the blind round, and say what the label did.

activities.title: Same Symptom, Different Cause: five tired people
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. Five made-up people all say, 'I am tired all the time.' You read one clue card for each. You find out that one symptom can have five different causes.

materials.item: paper slips, one for each person in the table
a pencil

activities.record: For each of the five people, write the likely cause and what would help. Then write one sentence: would one tonic help all five?

example_chart.title: Five people who feel tired all the time (copy each row on to a slip)
rows: Tired for two months. Pale inside her lower eyelids. Out of breath on the stairs. Eats mostly white rice, with tea at meals.
A doctor's blood test. Ragi, chana and greens with lemon. Iron tablets if the doctor says so.
Tired for three days. Fever and shivering every second day. Back from a forest trip with many mosquito bites.
Malaria, from a parasite carried by mosquitoes
A blood test today, and the antimalarial medicine a doctor orders.
Tired for a week. Goes to bed at half past eleven and wakes at six.
Sleep for ten hours. No medicine is needed.
Tired for months. Very thirsty. Passes urine many times a day and at night.
Diabetes: sugar stays in the blood
A blood sugar test. Changes in food, daily walking, and the medicines a doctor orders.
Tired for two months. A cough for more than three weeks. Losing weight. Sweating at night.
A spit test, and six months of free medicines from a government centre.

setup.art: Five paper slips face down on a table, each with a small drawing of a tired face on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Copy each person's clues on to a slip. Keep the last two columns of the table covered.

setup.art: A child holding one slip and writing a guess in a notebook, with four more slips waiting.
setup.caption: 2. Read one slip at a time. Write the likely cause, and what would help.

flow.do: 1. Say only this: five people each tell a doctor, 'I am tired all the time.' 2. Ask the question below. 3. Write down the answer and the reason.
flow.say: Five people say they are tired all the time. A shop sells a tonic for tiredness. Should all five take it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five people feel tired all the time. Should they all take the same tonic? Why?
flow.parent: Any answer with a reason is a good start. Do not correct it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Symptom, Different Cause. You decide whether five tired people need the same remedy, before you read any clues.

flow.do: 1. Your child reads the first slip aloud. 2. They say which kind of cause it points to: a germ, a missing nutrient, a body part, harm from outside or the way of life. 3. They say what would help. 4. Uncover that row of the table and compare. 5. Repeat for all five.
flow.say: Read the clues. What do you think is the cause? Which clue told you? What would help this person?
flow.kid: Read a slip. What is the cause? Which clue told you? What would help?

ask.q: Which clue told you that the girl of 12 is short of iron?
good: She is pale and out of breath.
She eats mostly white rice.
Tea at meals stops the body taking in iron.

flow.parent: Your child does not need to name the disease. Naming the kind of cause is enough. Say that a real diagnosis always needs a doctor and usually a test.
flow.context: In this step of Same Symptom, Different Cause you read the clues for each tired person. You work out the cause.

flow.do: Lay the five slips in a row. Ask whether one tonic could help all five, and what the tonic might hide.
flow.say: Look at all five. Could one tonic help them all? What might happen to the man with the cough if the tonic made him feel a little better?
flow.kid: Could one tonic help all five? What could go wrong for the man with the cough?

check.q: Five people have the same symptom, tiredness, from five different causes. What does each person need?
options: A treatment that fits their own cause
The same tonic for tiredness
The strongest medicine in the shop
check.why: A treatment works on a cause. Iron helps the girl and does nothing for malaria. If you chose the tonic, think of the man with tuberculosis. Feeling a little better could keep him away from the test he needs. A strong medicine for the wrong cause brings side effects and no benefit.

flow.context: This is the last step of Same Symptom, Different Cause. You decide what one remedy for a symptom can and cannot do.

activities.title: Read the Label: what a made-up medicine label tells you
activities.context: In this activity you read the label of a made-up syrup, printed in the table below. You find the name of the substance, the dose, the times, the expiry date and the warnings. No real medicine is touched. Real medicines are read and given by a grown-up.

materials.item: the made-up label in the table below
a notebook, a pencil and a clock or watch

activities.safety: This label is made up for practice. Real medicines are handled only by a grown-up, who follows the doctor and the real label.
activities.record: Write the answers to the six questions. Then write the three lines on the label that you think matter most, and why.

example_chart.title: A made-up label: SUNNY syrup (not a real medicine)
rows: Dose for a child of 10 to 15 kg
Dose for a child of 16 to 25 kg
Dose for a child of 26 to 35 kg
Every 6 hours if needed. Not more than 4 doses in 24 hours.
Not for more than 3 days without asking a doctor.
Shake well. Use the measuring cup provided.
May cause sleepiness. Keep out of reach of children.
Rx. To be sold only on the prescription of a doctor.
Store below 25 degrees Celsius, away from sunlight.

setup.art: A drawn label for a syrup bottle with a sun logo, lines of small print and a dose table, lying flat on a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Read the made-up label in the table, line by line.

setup.art: A child pointing at one line of a printed table with a pencil and writing an answer in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Find the generic name, the dose for a weight, the gap between doses and the expiry date.

flow.do: 1. Say that the label is made up. 2. Ask how many different facts a medicine label needs to give. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: This label is for a made-up syrup. Before you read it, guess. How many different things must a label tell the grown-up who gives the medicine?
flow.kid: This label is made up. Guess how many things a label must tell a grown-up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Label. You guess how many facts a medicine label must carry.

flow.do: Your child answers these six questions from the label. 1. What is the generic name? 2. What is the dose for a child of 22 kilograms? 3. A dose is given at 2.15 in the afternoon. What is the earliest time for the next? 4. What is the most syrup a 22-kilogram child may have in 24 hours? 5. Would this bottle be safe to use in April 2027? 6. Who decides whether the child should have it at all?
flow.say: Find each answer on the label. Show me the line you used.
flow.kid: Answer the six questions. Point to the line you used each time.

ask.q: What is the most a child of 22 kilograms may have in 24 hours?
good: 30 millilitres. That is 4 doses, and each dose is 7.5 millilitres.

ask.q: What is the earliest time for the next dose after 2.15 in the afternoon?
good: 8.15 in the evening, which is 6 hours later.

flow.parent: Answers: 1. Pretendol. 2. 7.5 millilitres. 3. 8.15 in the evening. 4. 30 millilitres, which is 4 doses of 7.5. 5. No. The expiry is February 2027. 6. A doctor, because the label says Rx. A grown-up then gives it.
flow.context: In this step of Read the Label you answer six questions from the made-up label.

flow.do: Ask the two questions below, and then the check.
flow.say: The measuring cup is lost. May the grown-up use a kitchen teaspoon? And why does the dose depend on the child's weight?
flow.kid: The measuring cup is lost. Is a kitchen spoon good enough? Why not?

ask.q: Why does a heavier child get a bigger dose?
good: The medicine spreads through a bigger body, so it is weaker in the blood.
The same spoonful makes a thinner mixture in a bigger body.

flow.parent: A kitchen teaspoon may hold 3 millilitres or 7, so it is not a measure. A chemist will give a measuring cup or a marked dropper.

check.q: A label says 'every 6 hours, not more than 4 doses in 24 hours'. A dose was missed. What should the grown-up do?
options: Give the usual dose and ask the doctor or chemist
Give two doses together
Give doses every 3 hours to catch up
check.why: Two doses together, or doses close together, push the level in the blood higher than the makers planned. In the Half-Glass Test, double doses took the tea to almost twice the level. A grown-up gives the usual amount and asks the doctor or the chemist what to do about the missed one.

flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Label. You say why the dose is measured exactly and why it depends on weight.

activities.title: The Medicine's Journey: draw the route of a swallowed tablet
activities.context: In this activity you draw a body outline and trace the path of a swallowed tablet. You draw it from the mouth to the blood, to the place where it works, and out of the body. You also mark where an inhaler, eye drops and an ointment go in.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, such as an opened newspaper page or the back of a calendar sheet
a pencil, and red, blue and green crayons or sketch pens

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Under it, write in one sentence why a tablet for a headache also reaches the toes.

setup.art: A child drawing the outline of a body on a large sheet of paper on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the outline of a body, with a mouth, a stomach, intestines, a liver, a heart and two kidneys.

setup.art: The same outline with a red dotted line running from the mouth through the stomach and intestine to the liver and heart, and red arrows spreading to the head, arms and legs.
setup.caption: 2. In red, draw the tablet's path in: mouth, stomach, small intestine, blood, liver, heart, everywhere.

setup.art: The same outline with a blue dotted line from the liver to the kidneys and the bladder, and small green arrows at the lungs, an eye and the skin of one arm.
setup.caption: 3. In blue, draw the path out through the liver and kidneys. In green, mark where an inhaler, eye drops and an ointment go in.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a body outline, about as long as their arm. 2. Ask the question below. 3. They draw their own idea of the path in pencil.
flow.say: A person with a sore toe swallows a tablet. How does the medicine get from the mouth to the toe? Draw what you think happens inside.
flow.kid: A tablet is swallowed for a sore toe. How does it reach the toe? Draw your idea.
flow.parent: Many children draw a tube from the stomach straight to the sore place. Keep the drawing. Do not correct it yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Medicine's Journey. You draw your own idea of how a swallowed tablet reaches a sore toe.

flow.do: 1. Read out the real path, one stop at a time. 2. Your child draws it in red: mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, through the gut wall into the blood, liver, heart, then out to every part. 3. They draw red arrows to the head, the hands, the skin and the toes.
flow.say: The tablet dissolves in the stomach. In the small intestine the medicine passes into the blood. The blood goes to the liver, then the heart pumps it everywhere. Draw each stop.
flow.kid: Draw the real path in red. Mouth, stomach, small intestine, blood, liver, heart, everywhere.

ask.q: The medicine was meant for the toe. Where else did it go?
good: It goes everywhere the blood goes.
To the brain, the skin and the stomach too.

flow.context: In this step of the Medicine's Journey you draw the real path of a swallowed medicine.

flow.do: 1. In blue, your child draws the way out: the liver changes the medicine, the kidneys filter it from the blood, and it leaves in urine. 2. In green, they mark three other ways in: an inhaler to the lungs, drops on the eye and ointment on the skin.
flow.say: Now draw the way out in blue. Then mark in green where an inhaler, eye drops and an ointment go in. Why might a doctor choose one of those?
flow.kid: Draw the way out in blue. Mark an inhaler, eye drops and ointment in green.

ask.q: Why is an asthma medicine breathed in and not swallowed?
good: It goes straight to the lungs, where it is needed.
A much smaller dose is enough, so there are fewer side effects.

flow.context: In this step of the Medicine's Journey you draw how a medicine leaves the body. You also mark three other ways in.

flow.do: Put the pencil drawing from the first step beside the coloured one. Ask what changed, and then the check.
flow.say: Compare your first idea with the real path. What is the biggest difference? What does the real path explain about side effects?
flow.kid: Compare your first drawing with the real path. What is different?

check.q: A swallowed medicine for a blocked nose makes a person sleepy. What explains this best?
options: Blood carries the medicine to the brain too
The medicine was too old
The nose is joined to the eyes
check.why: A swallowed medicine enters the blood, and blood goes to every organ. If the medicine fits molecules in the brain as well as in the nose, it acts in both places. An old medicine may work less well, but that does not explain sleepiness.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Medicine's Journey. You compare your first idea with the real path, and link the path to side effects.

activities.title: The Worst Day: read the chart of a cold
activities.context: In this activity you draw a line graph of an ordinary cold over ten days. Nobody in the graph took any remedy. Then you mark the day when people usually take a remedy, and read what happens next.

materials.item: squared paper, or a notebook page ruled into squares
a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Keep the graph. Under it, write what a person who took a remedy on day 3 would believe. Write why they would be mistaken.

example_chart.title: How bad an ordinary cold feels, with no remedy (0 is fine, 10 is the worst)

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper with days 1 to 10 along the bottom and 0 to 10 up the side, and a child plotting dots.
setup.caption: 1. Plot the ten numbers from the table as dots, and join them with a line.

setup.art: The finished line graph rising to a peak on day 3 and falling to zero on day 10, with a small spoon drawn at the peak.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the worst day. Read how the cold feels one day and two days later.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws two axes: days 1 to 10 along the bottom, and 0 to 10 up the side. 2. They plot the ten numbers from the table and join the dots. 3. Say that nobody in this chart took any remedy.
flow.say: This table shows an ordinary cold with no remedy. Plot each day as a dot and join the dots. What shape do you get?
flow.kid: Plot the ten numbers as dots. Join them. What shape is the line?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Worst Day. You draw a line graph of an ordinary cold that gets no remedy.

flow.do: 1. Ask on which day a person is most likely to reach for a remedy. 2. Your child draws a small spoon on that day. 3. They read the numbers for the next two days.
flow.say: On which day would most people reach for a remedy? Mark it. Now read the chart. How will the person feel two days later, whatever they took?
flow.kid: Which day would people take a remedy? Mark it. How do they feel two days later?

ask.q: The person took a remedy on day 3 and felt much better by day 5. What will they say about the remedy?
good: That it worked.
That it cured them in two days.

flow.parent: Day 3 is the worst day, at 8. By day 5 the number has fallen to 5 with no remedy. Any remedy taken at the peak is followed by improvement.
flow.context: In this step of the Worst Day you mark the day when people take remedies. Then you read what the chart says comes next.

flow.do: Read out the advertisement below, and ask the questions.
flow.say: An advertisement says that nine of ten people felt better within three days of taking a tonic. Is that evidence that the tonic works? What else would you ask?
flow.kid: An advert says nine in ten felt better in three days. Is that evidence? What would you ask?

ask.q: What would you ask the makers of the tonic?
good: How many people who took nothing felt better in three days?
Who counted, and did they know who took the tonic?

check.q: People usually take a remedy on the worst day of a cold. Why do they nearly always feel better soon after?
options: After the worst day, a cold improves anyway
Remedies work best on the worst day
The cold germs fear the remedy
check.why: The worst day is a peak, and after a peak the line goes down. So improvement follows the worst day whether a remedy was taken or not. If you chose the second answer, look at your graph. It shows the same fall with no remedy at all.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Worst Day. You judge an advertisement, using your graph.

activities.title: The Potato's New Skin: can a living thing close a wound with no medicine?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up cuts a raw potato, and you watch the cut face for three days. A raw potato is alive, and left alone they would sprout. You find out what a living potato does to a wound when nothing is put on it.

materials.item: a firm raw potato with no green patches
a knife, for the grown-up
a plate
thin paper, such as a strip of newspaper or tissue

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Do not eat this potato afterwards.

schedule.what: A grown-up cuts a potato in half. Test the wet cut face with paper and a fingertip. Leave one half cut face up in the open air.
Test the cut face again. A grown-up makes a fresh cut beside the old one, and you compare the two faces.

activities.record: Draw the cut face on day 1 and on day 3. Write what the paper strip showed each time, and what you found under the new skin.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a raw potato in half on a board, with a child watching.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a raw potato in half. Press a paper strip on the wet cut face.

setup.art: Half a potato on a plate on an open shelf, cut face up, away from the window.
setup.caption: 2. Leave one half on a plate, cut face up, in the open air for two days.

setup.art: A potato half with a dry, darker, leathery cut face, and beside it a freshly cut wet white face on the same piece.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, test the old face. A grown-up cuts a new face beside it. Compare the two.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the potato in half. 2. Your child presses a strip of paper on the cut face for ten seconds, and looks at the strip. 3. They rub a fingertip across the face. 4. Put one half on a plate, cut face up, on an open shelf out of the sun. 5. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: A raw potato is alive. I have just wounded this one. Nothing will be put on the cut. What will the cut face be like in two days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Press paper on the cut potato. Rub the face. What will it be like in two days? Why?
flow.parent: The fresh face wets the paper and leaves white starch on the fingertip. Do not cover the potato. In a closed box the face stays wet and mould grows.
flow.wait: Leave the potato half in the open air for two days
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato's New Skin. You test the fresh cut face of a raw potato, and guess what the potato will do.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, your child presses a new paper strip on the old cut face and rubs a fingertip across. 2. A grown-up cuts a thin slice off one edge of the piece. This makes a fresh face beside the old one. 3. Your child tests the fresh face in the same way. 4. They compare the two faces.
flow.say: Test the old cut face as you did on the first day. Now test this fresh cut beside it. What has the potato done to the old wound?
flow.kid: Test the old cut face. Then test a fresh cut. What has the potato done?

ask.q: How is the old face different from the fresh one?
good: It is dry and tough, like thin leather.
The paper stays dry.
It is darker, and no starch comes off.

flow.parent: The old face is usually dry, darker and firm, and the paper stays dry. Under a thin layer the flesh is still wet and white. If the old face has mould spots or is soft, the air was too damp. Throw the piece away and try again in a drier place.
flow.context: In this step of the Potato's New Skin you compare a cut face two days old with a fresh cut on the same potato.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Who closed the potato's wound?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Nothing was put on the cut. So what closed it?
good: The potato's own living cells.
The cells near the cut made a new layer.

flow.parent: The reason: the living cells just under the cut build a corky layer, much like the potato's skin. The layer keeps water in and microbes out. Farmers who cut seed potatoes leave the pieces for a few days so that this layer forms before planting. Your skin does a similar job on a scrape. It forms a scab, and new skin grows underneath. No ointment builds the new skin. An ointment can only keep germs out while the skin works.
flow.think: A boiled potato is no longer alive. What do you think happens to a cut in a boiled potato?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Potato's New Skin. You say what the potato did to a wound with no medicine.

projects.title: The Claim Collector: eight health claims and four questions
projects.context: In this three-day project you collect eight health claims from packets, advertisements and phone messages. You put four questions to each claim, and give it stars for its evidence. Then you make a one-page guide for your family.

materials.item: packets from your kitchen and bathroom, such as a health drink, a toothpaste, a soap, an oil or a breakfast food
old newspapers or magazines, and a grown-up to show you advertisements and forwarded messages
a notebook and a pencil
a sheet of chart paper or plain paper, and sketch pens

projects.safety: A grown-up chooses which phone messages and advertisements you see. Do not open or taste anything to test a claim.

schedule.what: Collect eight health claims and copy their exact words.
Ask four questions of each claim, and give each claim stars.
Make a one-page guide to the four questions, and explain it to your family.

projects.record: Make a table with a row for each claim: the exact words, where you found them, your answers to the four questions, and the stars. Keep the one-page guide where the family can see it.

setup.art: A child copying words from the back of a health drink jar into a notebook, with a toothpaste carton and a newspaper beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: copy eight health claims, word for word, and note where each came from.

setup.art: A notebook table with eight rows, four narrow columns headed with question marks and a column of small stars.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: ask four questions of each claim, and give one star for each good answer.

setup.art: A hand-drawn poster with four large numbered questions, pinned beside a fridge.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: make a one-page guide to the four questions, and explain it to your family.

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Your child looks for health claims on packets, in advertisements and in messages you choose to show. 2. They copy eight claims in their exact words. 3. They note where each came from. 4. Ask which claim they believe most, and why.
flow.say: A health claim says that something makes you healthier, stronger or safer from illness. Find eight, and copy the exact words. Which one do you believe most? Why?
flow.kid: Find eight health claims. Copy the exact words. Which do you believe most? Why?
flow.parent: Useful words to look for: 'boosts immunity', 'clinically proven', 'doctors recommend', 'kills 99.9 percent of germs', 'makes bones strong', 'no side effects'.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Claim Collector. You collect eight health claims and copy their exact words.

flow.do: Day 2. For each claim, your child asks four questions. 1. Compared with what? 2. How many people were tested? 3. Who measured, and did they know who got what? 4. Who is telling me, and what do they gain? They give one star for each question the claim answers well.
flow.say: Ask each claim four questions. Compared with what? How many people? Who measured? Who is telling me, and what do they gain? Give a star for each good answer.
flow.kid: Ask each claim the four questions. Give one star for each good answer.

ask.q: A packet says 'clinically proven'. Which of the four questions does it answer?
good: None, unless it says how many people and compared with what.
It only tells me that the maker wants me to buy it.

flow.parent: Most packet claims earn no stars or one, because they give no numbers at all. A claim with few stars is not proved false. It is simply not yet shown to be true. In India, a law of 1954 forbids advertisements that claim to cure certain diseases.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Claim Collector. You put four questions to each claim and give it stars for its evidence.

flow.do: Day 3. 1. Your child writes the four questions large on one page, with one example claim under each. 2. They explain the page to the family. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Make a one-page guide to the four questions. Then explain it to the family. Which of your eight claims had the most stars? What would change your mind about the others?
flow.kid: Write the four questions on one page. Explain them to your family.

check.q: A tonic's label says 'trusted by millions'. Which question does that leave unanswered?
options: Compared with what?
Is the tonic popular?
Is the bottle full?
check.why: Millions of buyers show that a tonic sells. They do not show what happens to people who do not take it. Without a comparison, nobody knows what the tonic adds.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Claim Collector. You make a one-page guide to the four questions and explain it to your family.

challenges.title: The Lid a Toddler Cannot Open
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about keeping medicines away from small children. You build a closure for a box that needs two actions at once. Rajma seeds stand for tablets, and no real medicine is used.
challenges.problem: Every year, small children are poisoned by tablets that they find and swallow. A toddler can pull, twist or press, but usually does only one action at a time. A grandmother may have stiff fingers. Design a closure for a small box. A toddler must fail to open it, and a grown-up must open it within 10 seconds.
constraints: The box holds 10 rajma seeds as pretend tablets. No real medicine is used.
Opening must need two different actions at the same time, or two actions in a set order.
A grown-up who has never seen the box must open it within 10 seconds, after reading one line of instructions.
No key, no tool and no knot that needs strong fingers.
materials: a small plastic or steel box with a lid, and a second, larger box
rubber bands, string, clothes pegs and a strip of cloth
card from an old carton, scissors and tape
a watch or a phone timer
general: A lid that must be pressed down and turned at the same time, as on many real medicine bottles.
A lid held by two rubber bands that must be pulled apart with both hands.
A box inside a box, with the two lids opening in opposite directions.
creative: A lid that lifts only when two painted marks are lined up.
A card sleeve that slides off only while two clothes pegs are squeezed together.
A latch set deep in a card tube, which only a long grown-up finger can reach.

ask.q: Why does a lid that needs two actions at once stop most toddlers?
good: A toddler tries one action, then another, but seldom both together.
A toddler has not yet learned to plan two movements at once.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the better design. 2. They write one line of instructions on the box. 3. A grown-up who has not seen it opens the box, and your child times this. 4. Your child tries to open it with one hand, one action at a time.

flow.kid: Build your design. Write one instruction. Time a grown-up. Then try with one hand.
flow.parent: If you needed more than 10 seconds, the design fails for a grown-up. If your child can open it with one action, it fails for a toddler. Either result is useful. Never test the box on a real toddler.

flow.say: What would you change? And here is a harder question. Is a clever lid enough to keep a toddler safe?
flow.kid: What would you change? Is a clever lid enough to keep a toddler safe?
flow.parent: Dr Henri Breault, a Canadian children's doctor, pushed for the press-and-turn cap in 1967. Poisonings of small children fell sharply where it was used.

check.q: What keeps a toddler safest from the medicines in a home?
options: Locked away or high up, in closed packets
A lid that is hard to open, left on a table
Telling the toddler not to touch
check.why: A hard lid only slows a child down, and lids are often left loose. A toddler cannot be relied on to obey. Medicines kept locked or out of reach cannot be found at all. The hard lid is the second line of safety.

challenges.title: Plan a Fair Trial of a Kashaya
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge on paper. A kashaya is a hot drink of pepper, ginger and tulsi that many families take for a cold. In the story Across the Stream, some children drank it and some did not. Both groups were well in the same seven days. You plan a real trial that could test it properly.
challenges.problem: People say that a kashaya cures a cold. Plan a trial, on paper, that could find out two things. Does the kashaya shorten a cold? Does the kashaya ease the cough at night? Real trials on people are run only by doctors, with the agreement of every family. Your job is the plan.
constraints: At least 40 children with colds take part, and their parents agree.
Chance decides who gets the kashaya.
The other group gets a warm drink that looks and tastes as similar as possible.
The person who counts the coughs must not know who drank what.
No child is kept away from a doctor. Any child with a fever for three days leaves the trial and is seen by one.
Decide what you will measure before the trial starts.
materials: the five things a fair trial needs: two groups, chance, a dummy, blind counting and many people
general: Toss a coin for each child: heads for kashaya, tails for the other drink.
Parents write down each morning whether the child still has a cold.
Count the days until each child is well, and compare the averages of the two groups.
creative: Make the dummy drink from black tea and jaggery with a pinch of pepper. It will be dark and a little hot.
Record each child's night with a phone, and let someone who does not know the groups count the coughs.
Pair children of the same age, and toss one coin for each pair, so that the groups match.
Give each child the kashaya for one cold and the dummy for the next, and compare.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own plan as a chart with boxes and arrows. Start at 'find 40 children' and end at 'compare the two groups'. Write what you will measure. Then write one thing your trial cannot tell you.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a flow chart: one box at the top splitting by a coin into two boxes, each leading to a box marked 'count'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the trial as boxes and arrows: the children, the coin, the two drinks, the counting.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Ask what is wrong with simply giving the kashaya to 40 children and counting how many get well. 3. Write the answer.
flow.say: Suppose we gave the kashaya to forty children with colds, and all forty were well in ten days. What would that show? What is missing?
flow.kid: Forty children drink kashaya. All are well in ten days. What does that show?

ask.q: What is missing from a trial with one group?
good: Children who did not drink it, to compare.
Colds end in about a week anyway.

flow.context: This is the first step of Plan a Fair Trial of a Kashaya. You say what a trial with only one group cannot show.

flow.do: Your child plans the two groups, how chance will choose, and what the second group will drink. They write what will be measured, and by whom.
flow.say: Plan the two groups. How will chance choose? What will the second group drink, so that nobody can tell? What will you measure, and who will measure it?
flow.kid: Plan two groups. Let chance choose. Plan the dummy drink. Decide what to measure.

ask.q: Why must the second group's drink look and taste similar?
good: So the children and parents cannot tell which group they are in.
Knowing could change what they say about the cough.

flow.parent: A perfect dummy for a strong-tasting drink is hard to make. Real trials of foods and herbs have the same trouble. Saying so is a good answer.
flow.context: In this step of Plan a Fair Trial of a Kashaya you plan the groups, the dummy and the measuring.

flow.do: Your child draws the plan as boxes and arrows, and adds the safety rule for a child who gets worse.
flow.say: Draw your plan as boxes and arrows. Where does the coin come in? Where is the blind counting? What happens to a child who gets worse?
flow.kid: Draw your plan as boxes and arrows. Add the rule for a child who gets worse.
