flow.do: Ask what the trial cannot tell, and then the check.
flow.say: Suppose both groups are well in seven days, but the kashaya group coughs less at night. What would you say the kashaya does? What can your trial not tell you?
flow.kid: Both groups are well in seven days. One coughs less at night. What does the kashaya do?

check.q: In a trial of a cold remedy, both groups are well in seven days. The remedy group slept better. What does the remedy do?
options: It eases a symptom, and does not shorten the cold
It cures the cold
It does nothing at all
check.why: The cold lasted the same time in both groups, so the remedy did not remove the cause. Better sleep is a real benefit, and it is an eased symptom. 'Cures' claims too much, and 'nothing' claims too little.

flow.context: This is the last step of Plan a Fair Trial of a Kashaya. You say what a result would mean, and what the trial cannot tell.

items.p: What is the cause of a disease?
opts: The thing that makes the disease begin
items.why: A cause is what makes a disease begin, such as a germ or a missing nutrient. A symptom is only what the disease shows. If you chose the symptom, remember that one symptom can come from many causes.

items.p: Sort these diseases by their kind of cause.
items.why: Malaria and typhoid are caused by germs. Anaemia comes from too little iron, and goitre from too little iodine. In type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops making insulin, and in cataract the lens of the eye clouds.

items.p: Match each disease to the protection that prevents it.
items.why: Each protection blocks one cause. A net blocks the mosquito, safe water blocks the cholera germ, and iodised salt supplies the missing iodine.

items.p: A medicine that kills bacteria and does nothing to viruses is called an ____.
items.why: Antibiotics act on parts that bacteria have and viruses lack. So they cannot help a cold or flu.

items.p: Paracetamol lowers a fever by killing the germ that caused the fever.
items.why: False. Paracetamol eases the symptom. The germ is untouched, and the body's defenders or another medicine must deal with it.

items.p: What does insulin do for a person with type 1 diabetes?
opts: Replaces what the pancreas no longer makes
items.why: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops making insulin. The injected insulin does that missing job each day. No germ causes diabetes, and insulin does not repair the pancreas.

items.p: A swallowed tablet travels only to the part of the body that hurts.
items.why: False. The medicine passes into the blood, and the blood carries it to every part. This is why side effects happen.

items.p: The time a body takes to remove half of a medicine is called its ____.
items.why: After one half-life, half the medicine is left. After two, a quarter is left. The half-life decides how far apart the doses are.

items.p: A glass holds 4 teaspoons of tea. Half is poured away, twice. How many teaspoons are left?
items.why: Half of 4 is 2, and half of 2 is 1. A medicine in the body falls in the same way, by half in each half-life.

items.p: In the Wilted Stems Trial, why did a coin choose the glass for each stem?
opts: So nobody could pick the fresher stems
items.why: If a person chose, they might put the perkier stems in the sugar glass without meaning to. Chance treats both glasses alike. A coin does nothing to the stems themselves.

items.p: In the Wilted Stems Trial, what would the sugar glass alone have made you believe? Why is that a mistake?
items.a: I would have believed that sugar revives wilted stems, because they stood up. That is a mistake, because the stems in plain water stood up just as well. The water revived them and the sugar added nothing.
items.why: A strong answer says that recovery after a treatment needs a comparison group. It uses the plain water glass as the evidence.

items.p: A cold ended a week after a remedy. Give two reasons why this does not show that the remedy worked.
items.a: First, a cold ends by itself in about a week. Second, people take a remedy on the worst day, and after the worst day a cold improves anyway. Only a comparison with children who took nothing could show what the remedy added.
items.why: A strong answer names getting better anyway, and says what evidence would be needed.

items.p: Draw the path of a swallowed tablet through the body, from the mouth to the urine. Label five stops.
items.a: Mouth, stomach, small intestine, blood and liver, then the heart pumps it everywhere. The liver changes it, the kidneys filter it out, and it leaves in urine.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the medicine passing into the blood and reaching the whole body. It also shows the liver and kidneys removing it.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body with five empty label lines.

items.p: A child has an ordinary cold. Should the family give a home remedy?

views.says: My pepper rasam has soothed colds in this family for fifty years. It warms the throat and helps the child sleep.
A cold ends by itself. A warm drink does no harm. But a fever beyond three days, or fast breathing, needs me.
The cold will end in a week whatever you do. So a remedy is a waste of effort.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The grandmother is right that easing a symptom is a real help. The neighbour is right that the cold is not shortened. The doctor adds the limit: some illnesses do not end by themselves.
items.why: All three speakers say something true. A strong answer keeps apart two things: shortening the illness and easing the symptoms.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair trial in order.
items: Chance puts the people into two groups
Find many people who agree to take part
Measure everyone without knowing their group
One group gets the medicine and one gets a dummy
a: Find many people who agree to take part
Chance puts the people into two groups
One group gets the medicine and one gets a dummy
Measure everyone without knowing their group
items.why: People must agree first. Chance makes the groups alike. The dummy and the blind measuring keep hopes from changing the result. The comparison comes last.

items.p: You find a loose tablet on the floor at home. What should you do?
opts: Taste it to find out what it is
Put it back in any bottle
items.why: A child never tastes or takes a medicine alone. A tablet in the wrong bottle could be given to the wrong person. A tablet left on the floor could be found by a smaller child.

items.p: Why is a dose of a medicine repeated after some hours?
opts: The body removes the medicine all the time
The first dose is always too weak
items.why: The liver and kidneys start removing a medicine as soon as it arrives. After a few hours too little is left to work, so another dose is needed.

items.p: In the Half-Glass Test, why did the tea stop rising near 4 teaspoons?
opts: Loss at each pour equalled one dose
The spoon held less each time
items.why: A pour removes half of what is there. At 4 teaspoons a pour removes 2, and the dose adds 2, so the level stays. The glass was filled to the same line every time.

items.p: A glass holds 6 teaspoons of tea. Half is poured away, and 4 are added. How many teaspoons now?
items.why: Half of 6 is 3. Adding the dose of 4 makes 7.

items.p: Taking two doses together is a safe way to make up for a missed dose.
items.why: False. Two doses together push the level in the blood higher than was planned. A grown-up asks the doctor or the chemist what to do.

items.p: An inhaler needs a smaller dose than a tablet, because its medicine goes straight to the lungs.
items.why: True. A swallowed medicine is spread through the whole body. A breathed-in medicine lands where it is needed, so far less is enough.

items.p: Three of these are needed for a fair trial. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A trial needs a comparison group, chance and blind measuring. A famous person's support tells us nothing about whether a medicine works.

items.p: Match each medicine to the job it does.
pairs: Replaces what the pancreas no longer makes
items.why: Each medicine does one exact job. None of them does the body's repair work.

items.p: Sort these jobs. Is each one done by the treatment, or by the body?
items: holding the edges of a cut together
growing new skin across a cut
items.why: An antibiotic, stitches and an iron tablet each do one job. Growing skin, bone and blood cells is done only by living cells.

items.p: A dummy treatment with no medicine in it, used in trials, is called a ____.
items.why: A placebo looks and tastes like the real treatment. It lets the control group expect the same as the treated group.

items.p: In a trial, the doctor chooses which patients get the new medicine. Explain how this could spoil the trial.
items.a: Without meaning to, the doctor might give the new medicine to the patients who look stronger. Then the groups differ before the trial starts. A difference at the end could come from the choosing and not from the medicine.
items.why: A strong answer says the groups must be alike at the start, and that only chance makes them alike.

items.p: In the Label Test, both cups held the same drink. Explain why their scores can still differ.
items.a: The label told the tasters to expect a sweeter drink. The brain builds a taste from the tongue's signal and from what it expects. So an honest taster can score the labelled cup higher.
items.why: A strong answer says that expecting something changes what a person reports, and links this to why trials are blind.

items.p: A swallowed medicine for a blocked nose can make a person sleepy. Explain why.
items.a: The medicine passes into the blood, and the blood carries it to every part of the body. In the brain its molecules also fit, and there they cause sleepiness.
items.why: A strong answer says that a swallowed medicine goes everywhere. A side effect is the same medicine acting in another place.

items.p: In a trial of a new medicine, should half of the ill people get a dummy?

views.says: I am ill now. If there is a new medicine, I want the medicine and not a dummy.
Nobody yet knows whether the new medicine helps or harms. Only a comparison can tell us. Everyone still gets the usual care.

views.who: A person who falls ill ten years later
views.says: I need to know which medicines truly work. I depend on the people who took part in the trials.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the patient: wanting the best chance is fair. For the doctor: an untested medicine may be worse than the dummy, as bloodletting was. For the later patient: without trials, useless treatments last for centuries.
items.why: This is a real question that doctors argue about. A strong answer notices that the new medicine is not yet known to be better.

items.p: On a body outline, label where each goes in: a tablet, an inhaler, eye drops, an ointment.
a: Tablet: the mouth, then the gut and the blood
items.why: A tablet reaches the whole body through the blood. The other three put the medicine at the place where it is needed.
items.art: An outline of a child's head and upper body with four blank label lines pointing to the mouth, the chest, one eye and one forearm.

items.p: Which sentence about a 'natural' remedy is true?
opts: It can still have side effects
It works because it is old
items.why: A plant strong enough to change the body is strong enough to harm it. Datura is natural and poisonous. Old or natural remedies need the same fair trial as any medicine.

items.p: Twenty people took a syrup and all recovered. What is the most important thing still unknown?
opts: How many recover without the syrup
items.why: If twenty similar people who took nothing also recovered, the syrup added nothing. Without that comparison the twenty recoveries show very little.

items.p: A trial has only six people in each group. Why is that weak evidence?
opts: Luck can decide the result in small groups
items.why: With six in a group, one or two people who recover by luck change the result a great deal. With hundreds, luck evens out.

items.p: In the 2011 asthma trial, what did a dummy inhaler change?
opts: How patients felt, and not their measured breathing
Both their feeling and their breathing
items.why: Patients said they felt better after the dummy inhaler. A breathing meter showed that their airways had opened only after the real one.

items.p: A remedy that has been used for a thousand years must work.
items.why: False. Bloodletting was used for about two thousand years and did harm. A useless remedy can last for centuries, because most of its patients get better anyway.

items.p: A fair trial can show that a treatment does not work.
items.why: True. If the treated group does no better than the control group, the treatment added nothing. Trials showed this for antibiotics against colds.

items.p: In a trial, 4 of the 55 patients given a new medicine died. How many of the 55 lived?
items.why: 55 take away 4 is 51. In the group of 52 given bed rest alone, 14 died and 38 lived.

items.p: Put these in order, from the weakest evidence to the strongest.
items: Two groups chosen by chance, measured blind
Two groups chosen by the doctor
Twenty recovered patients and no second group
a: Twenty recovered patients and no second group
Two groups chosen by the doctor
Two groups chosen by chance, measured blind
items.why: One story is the weakest. Twenty counted patients are better, but have no comparison. A doctor's choice gives a comparison that may be tilted. Chance and blind measuring remove the tilt.

items.p: An illness that the body ends by itself within days is called a ____ illness.
items.why: A cold is self-limiting. Any remedy taken during such an illness seems to work.

items.p: An advertisement says nine in ten users felt better in three days. Write two questions to ask the makers.
items.a: How many people who used nothing felt better in three days? Who counted, and did they know who had used the product? Other good questions: how many people were asked, and who paid for the count?
items.why: A strong answer asks for a comparison group and asks who measured.

items.p: Doses of 2 teaspoons, halved each time, level off near 4. Predict the level for doses of 3. Explain.
items.a: Near 6 teaspoons. At 6 teaspoons a pour removes 3, and the dose adds 3, so the level stays. The level settles at twice the dose.
items.why: A strong answer finds the level at which the amount removed equals the dose.

items.p: An ill chimpanzee chews a bitter plant and recovers. Is this evidence that the plant is a medicine? Explain.
items.a: It is a hint, and not strong evidence. She might have recovered anyway, and it is one case. It is a good reason to test the plant. The hint is stronger if ill chimpanzees choose the plant and healthy ones avoid the same plant.
items.why: A strong answer treats the case as a hint worth testing, and says what more would be needed.

items.p: A stitched cut joins in a week. Say what the stitches did, and what the skin did.
items.a: The stitches held the two edges together and kept dirt out. The skin cells divided and grew across the gap, and joined the edges. The stitches could not make new skin.
items.why: A strong answer gives the treatment one exact job and gives the repair to the living cells.

items.p: How should old remedies, such as those of Ayurveda and Siddha, be judged?

views.says: Every remedy must pass the same fair trial. Until it does, nobody knows whether it works or what harm it does.
We treat the whole person with food, routine and mixtures chosen for each patient. A trial of one extract does not test that.

views.who: A scientist who searches old books
views.says: Old remedies are good guesses by careful observers. Most will fail a trial. A few will become great medicines, as sarpagandha did.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: bloodletting lasted two thousand years. For the second: a trial can compare whole treatments too, if two groups are made by chance. For the third: sarpagandha and artemisinin both came from old texts, after testing.
items.why: This is a real disagreement in India today. A strong answer says what evidence each side would accept.

items.p: Draw a graph of the tea in the Half-Glass Test over six doses, before and after each dose.
items.a: A zigzag line. It jumps up by 2 teaspoons at each dose and falls by half before the next. The tops go 2, 3, 3 and a half, 3 and three-quarters, and then just under 4. The bottoms go 1, 1 and a half, and then just under 2.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the jumps staying the same size and the falls growing bigger. The zigzag levels off below 4.
items.art: Blank axes on squared paper, with dose numbers 1 to 6 along the bottom and 0 to 5 teaspoons up the side.

items.p: Match each observation to what it shows.
pairs: Stems in plain water recovered as well as stems in sugar water
Stems on the dry plate stayed limp
A labelled cup scored sweeter than the same drink unlabelled
The tea levelled off near 4 teaspoons
A fuller glass loses more at each pour
A cut potato face turned dry and tough
items.why: Each observation is evidence, and each conclusion says only what that evidence supports.

quiz.p: Three people have a fever. Why might each one need a different treatment?
opts: One symptom can have different causes
Each person needs the newest medicine
quiz.why: A fever is a symptom. Malaria, typhoid and flu each cause one, and each needs a different treatment. So the cause must be found first.

quiz.p: Which of these protects a sleeping family against malaria?
quiz.why: Malaria parasites are carried by mosquitoes who bite at night. A net blocks them. Boiled water blocks the germs of cholera and typhoid.

quiz.p: Which disease is cured by a nutrient, and not by a medicine that kills germs?
quiz.why: Goitre comes from too little iodine, and iodised salt prevents and treats it. The other three are caused by germs.

quiz.p: What does an antibiotic do to a cold virus?
quiz.why: An antibiotic acts on parts that bacteria have and viruses lack. A cold is caused by a virus, so the antibiotic has nothing to act on.

quiz.p: A broken arm is put in a plaster cast. What mends the bone?
quiz.why: The cast only holds the bone still. Bone cells bridge the break over some weeks. No medicine builds bone.

quiz.p: A swallowed medicine passes into the blood. Where does the blood carry it?
opts: To every part of the body
Only to the part that is ill
quiz.why: Blood reaches every organ, so the medicine does too. That is why a medicine can have effects in places it was not meant for.

quiz.p: A medicine has a half-life of 4 hours. How much of one dose is left after 8 hours?
quiz.why: After 4 hours half is left. After 4 more hours, half of that is left, which is a quarter.

quiz.p: A cough ended five days after a child took a syrup. What can we say?
opts: We cannot tell whether the syrup helped
The syrup made the cough last longer
quiz.why: Most coughs end by themselves. Without a group that took no syrup, nobody can say what the syrup added.

quiz.p: In a trial of a medicine, what is the control group for?
opts: To show what happens without the medicine
quiz.why: The control group gets a dummy. Whatever happens to them would have happened anyway, so the medicine's effect is the difference between the groups.

quiz.p: In a blind trial, the patients know whether they got the real medicine or the dummy.
quiz.why: False. Blind means the patients do not know. This keeps their hopes from changing what they report.

quiz.p: Who should give a child a medicine?
opts: A grown-up, in the way a doctor says
The child, if she can read the label
Anyone who had the same illness
quiz.why: A medicine needs the right cause, the right dose and the right times. A grown-up follows the doctor and the label. A child never takes a medicine alone.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: How much a dummy can change a disease
quiz.why: The other three are settled by strong evidence. How much a placebo can do, beyond changing what people feel and report, is still argued over.

People with diabetes, asthma or high blood pressure take medicines for decades and live full lives.
Jan Aushadhi shops across India sell tested generic medicines at much lower prices than the brands.

maths.problem: In the Half-Glass Test, the tea after each dose was 2, 3, 3.5 and 3.75 teaspoons. How far below 4 is each number? What is the pattern? Will the tea ever reach 4?
maths.answer: The gaps are 2, 1, 0.5 and 0.25. Each gap is half the one before. The tea gets closer and closer to 4 and never reaches it.
maths.explain: 4 take away 2 is 2. 4 take away 3 is 1. 4 take away 3.5 is 0.5. 4 take away 3.75 is 0.25. Each pour halves the gap. Half of something is never nothing, so the gap never closes completely.
maths.context: In the Half-Glass Test, a dose of 2 teaspoons of tea is added to a glass of water. Before each new dose, half the glass is poured away.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the gaps shows where the level is heading, without doing a hundred doses.

maths.problem: In the Half-Glass Test, one dose of 2 teaspoons goes in, and no more. Each pour removes half. How much tea is left after 1, 2, 3 and 4 pours? What fraction of the dose is that last amount?
maths.answer: 1 teaspoon, a half, a quarter and an eighth of a teaspoon. An eighth of a teaspoon is one-sixteenth of the dose.
maths.explain: Half of 2 is 1. Half of 1 is a half. Half of a half is a quarter. Half of a quarter is an eighth. The dose was 2 teaspoons, and an eighth is one-sixteenth of 2. Four halvings leave one-sixteenth.
maths.context: In the Half-Glass Test, tea stands for a medicine. Pouring away half the glass stands for the body removing the medicine.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again shows how quickly one dose fades, and why a second dose is needed.

maths.problem: In the Half-Glass Test, doses of 2 teaspoons levelled off near 4, and doses of 4 teaspoons near 8. Where would doses of 3 teaspoons level off? What is the rule?
maths.answer: Near 6 teaspoons. The level settles at twice the dose.
maths.explain: The level stops rising when a pour removes exactly one dose. A pour removes half. So the glass must hold twice the dose: 2 times 3 is 6. Check: half of 6 is 3, and 3 plus 3 is 6 again.
maths.context: In the Half-Glass Test, half the glass is poured away before each new dose of tea. The level of tea rises and then stays.
maths.why_maths: A rule that links the dose to the final level lets you predict a new case without testing it.

maths.problem: In the trial of 1948, 4 of 55 patients given streptomycin died, and 14 of 52 given bed rest alone. Write each as a percentage, to the nearest whole number. About how many times greater was the second?
maths.answer: About 7 percent of the first group died and about 27 percent of the second. The second share is nearly 4 times the first.
maths.explain: 4 divided by 55 is about 0.07, which is 7 percent. 14 divided by 52 is about 0.27, which is 27 percent. 27 divided by 7 is nearly 4.
maths.context: In 1948, doctors tested streptomycin, a new medicine for tuberculosis. Chance put 107 patients into two groups, and only one group got the medicine.
maths.why_maths: The two groups were different sizes. Percentages let us compare them fairly.

maths.problem: In a made-up run of the Wilted Stems Trial, glass A got 7 stems and glass B got 5. Six recovered in A and 4 in B. Which glass did better? Would you trust the difference?
maths.answer: Glass A did better, with about 86 percent recovered against 80 percent. I would not trust the difference, because one stem more or less would change the answer.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 7 is about 0.86. 4 divided by 5 is 0.80. But if one more stem in B had recovered, B would show 100 percent. A result that one stem can reverse is luck, and the trial needs more stems.
maths.context: In the Wilted Stems Trial, a coin sends limp coriander stems to sugar water or to plain water. You count how many stand up again.
maths.why_maths: Turning counts into percentages lets you compare groups of different sizes, and shows how little a small group can prove.

maths.problem: In a made-up Label Test, four tasters gave the ORDINARY cup 11 points in all. They gave the EXTRA SWEET cup 15. In the blind round, the two cups got 13 and 12. Find the average score for each cup. What did the label add?
maths.answer: With labels, the average for ORDINARY was 2.75 and for EXTRA SWEET 3.75. Without labels, the averages were 3.25 and 3. So the label added about 1 point for each taster.
maths.explain: 11 divided by 4 is 2.75. 15 divided by 4 is 3.75. The difference is 1. In the blind round, 13 divided by 4 is 3.25 and 12 divided by 4 is 3. The difference is only 0.25, which is small enough to be luck.
maths.context: In the Label Test, people taste two cups of the same lemon drink. In round 1 one cup is labelled EXTRA SWEET. In round 2 the cups have no labels.
maths.why_maths: An average gives one number for each cup, so that the two rounds can be compared.

maths.problem: In Read the Label, the made-up syrup may be given every 6 hours, at most 4 times in 24 hours. The first dose is at 7.30 in the morning. Write the earliest times of the next three doses. Another label says 'three times a day'. How many hours apart is that, spread evenly?
maths.answer: The next three doses are at 1.30 in the afternoon, 7.30 in the evening and 1.30 at night. Three times a day, spread evenly, means every 8 hours.
maths.explain: Add 6 hours each time: 7.30, 1.30, 7.30, 1.30. For three doses in a day, divide 24 hours by 3, which is 8. Doses bunched into the daytime leave a long gap at night, when the level falls low.
maths.context: In Read the Label you read the label of a made-up syrup. It gives the gap between doses and the most doses allowed in a day.
maths.why_maths: Working out clock times turns 'every 6 hours' into a plan that a family can follow.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people learn to tell a medicine that works from one that does not? This card tells the true story of a treatment that failed the test, and of the first fair trial.
how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, doctors in Europe and Asia treated fevers by bloodletting. They opened a vein and let out a bowl of blood. Patients often felt calmer afterwards, and most recovered, so nobody doubted the treatment. In 1835 a doctor in Paris, Pierre Louis, did something new. He counted. He compared 77 patients with pneumonia who had been bled early or late in their illness. More of those bled early died than of those bled late. But Louis could not decide who got which treatment. In 1948 the British scientist Austin Bradford Hill solved that problem. He planned a trial of streptomycin, a new medicine for tuberculosis. Random numbers in sealed envelopes put 107 patients into two groups. After six months, 4 of the 55 patients given streptomycin had died. Of the 52 given bed rest alone, about 14 had died. The doctors who read the chest X-rays did not know which group each patient was in. Since then, a new medicine is trusted only after such a trial.
how_we_found_out.who: Pierre Louis, a doctor in Paris. Austin Bradford Hill, a British scientist of statistics, with the doctors Marc Daniels and Philip D'Arcy Hart.
how_we_found_out.when: Louis published his counts in 1835. The streptomycin trial was published in October 1948.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That bloodletting cures fevers, because patients who were bled usually recovered. They recovered in spite of it. Louis's counts showed no clear benefit, and the 1948 trial showed how to test any treatment fairly: two groups, chosen by chance, counted by people who do not know the groups.
how_we_found_out.art: A doctor in an 1830s coat sitting at a desk covered with patient notes, drawing up two long columns of tally marks by lamplight.

roots.context: In this unit you ran a trial on wilted stems and watched a cut potato grow a new skin. Now we ask what healing tells us about ourselves and about living beings.

deep_truth.truth: In the Wilted Stems Trial, stems in plain water stood up as well as stems in sugar water. The stems recovered by drawing water back into their own cells. A body ends most colds and closes most cuts in the same way, by its own repair. A medicine removes a cause or supplies what is missing, and the body does the mending.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the medicine cured me', and give the bottle all the credit. People have done this for thousands of years, which is how useless remedies such as bloodletting lasted so long. A medicine does one exact job. The living cells of the body do the rest, and in many illnesses they do all of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Wilted Stems Trial, sugar water and plain water revive about the same number of stems. Stems on a dry plate stay limp. In the Potato's New Skin, a cut potato grows a tough new layer with nothing put on the cut. In trials, colds last about a week with a remedy or without one. If your own stems or your potato behaved differently, write down what you saw and try again.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that repairs itself all day. Scrapes close, colds end and bruises fade, mostly without your noticing or deciding.
three.what_is_life: Every living being mends themselves. A potato grows a new skin, a stem refills their cells, and an orangutan treats his own wound. Healing is something living beings do, and a medicine is help that they find or make.
three.what_is_this_world: One event follows another, and people easily take the first for the cause of the second. The world shows what caused what only when we compare, as the two glasses of stems did.

roots.thread: A cut potato, a limp stem and a child with a cold recover by the work of their own cells. Some other animals search out plants that help them when they are ill. People have learned to make medicines that each do one exact job. So a medicine is one living being's help to another being's own repair. The same power of repair runs through every living body. A doctor's skill is to know when a body needs help and when it needs only time.

science.text: Common colds and many other everyday illnesses are ended by the body's own defences, and remedies do not shorten them.
A wound is closed by the body's own cells. Medicines can keep germs out, but no medicine builds new skin or bone.
Whether a dummy treatment can change a disease, and not only how a person feels, is still argued over.
Chimpanzees and orangutans have been seen treating their own illnesses and wounds with plants. How they know which plant to use is not yet understood.

other_view.view: They would say that this gives the body too much credit. A child with type 1 diabetes dies without insulin. A person with tuberculosis usually dies without medicines. Before vaccines and antibiotics, a great many children died before they grew up. These doctors warn that people who trust the body to heal itself often wait too long. For them, a medicine is often the whole difference between living and dying.

practice.title: The scar that mended
practice.say: Find an old scar or a healed scratch on your body. Put one finger on it. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly, five times. Remember how it looked when it was new. You did not decide to mend it, and nobody mended it for you. Your cells did it while you played and slept. Somewhere in your body, cells are mending something now. Sit quietly for one minute, and thank them if you like.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. No part uses a real medicine. Tea, rajma seeds and a made-up label stand in for medicines. Every part says that only a grown-up gives a medicine, as a doctor says. The Half-Glass Test (core) needs four matching clear glasses and strong black tea. The amounts of tea are worked out by halving, and the colours should follow them. The colours of 1, 2 and 4 teaspoons differ clearly on white paper only if the tea is strong. The first step says how to check this. The pour removes half all at once, and a body removes a medicine little by little. So the glass is a model. The Wilted Stems Trial (core) needs fresh coriander and about three hours in all, most of it waiting. Limp stems usually stand up again in water within one to two hours, in sugar water and plain water alike. Stems that have dried crisp do not recover, and the steps say what to do then. With six stems in a glass, a difference of one stem is luck. The Label Test needs at least four willing tasters, and they must be told the truth afterwards. In some homes the label makes no difference, and the step says that this is a real result. In the Potato's New Skin, the cut face usually turns dry and tough in two days in open air. In very damp weather mould may grow instead, and the step says to try again in a drier place. Both card games were checked: Find the Cause has 16 cards for five mats. Tale, Hint or Trial has six cards for each of three mats. The Lid a Toddler Cannot Open must never be tested on a real toddler. Plan a Fair Trial of a Kashaya is a plan on paper only. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against published sources: the 1948 streptomycin trial (107 patients, 55 and 52), Rotavac (6,799 babies, Delhi, Pune, Vellore), the Madras trial (193 patients), Pierre Louis (77 patients), Sen and Bose 1931, Vakil 1949, Tu Youyou 1972, insulin in 1922, Chausiku in 1987, Rakus in 2022, and the placebo papers. Softened: the control deaths in 1948 (sources give 14 or 15), the Madras result, Vorderman's prison figures (exact ratios removed), Alice Ball's credit, and details of Kalunde and Rakus. Not re-checked: the Tirukkural, Charaka and Hippocratic passages are paraphrased. The health rules are general. A doctor who knows the child knows best. The three videos have no address yet.
